lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for The Lesson page. This page teaches you our big idea: some things are living, and some things are not living. Living things grow, eat, drink and can have babies. By the end you will be able to look at a thing and say "that is living" or "that is not living" — and say why. You need your eyes, your ears, your voice, and maybe a pencil. Let's start with something small. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. There are 4 concepts. Their names are Living or Not Living, What Living Things Need, Animals and Plants Are Alive, and Caring for Living Things. Read the first one slowly. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. Read and listen to all 4, one at a time. I expect you to go slowly and not skip any. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Each concept has an example at the end. Say the example out loud with your own voice. Then try it for real with things near you. For concept 1, find a stone and a leaf and make two piles: Living and Not Living. For concept 2, put your hand on your chest, breathe in, and say the four needs: food, water, air, warmth. For concept 3, look at a plant and say three signs it is alive. For concept 4, give a plant water or feed the chickens. I expect you to use your own real things and your own out-loud voice. That is how it sticks. Step 3. When you have read all 4 concepts, go to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it after you have really read them all. I expect honest work here — you are learning for you. Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same concepts. On the first slide, press Start. Use the same buttons on each slide, and press Listen if you want to hear it again. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to look at every slide, not rush to the end. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now go and do Step 1. Come back and tell me one thing you found that is living, and one thing that is not living. I will be right here! 🙂

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Science Words. On this page you will meet the special words for Unit 1, Being Alive. Words like Living, Non-living, Animal, Plant, Grow, Food and Water, Air and Warmth. We learn these words so you can say WHY something is alive, not just point at it. By the end you will be able to say each word, say what it means in your own words, and use it in a sentence. You need your eyes, your voice, your fingers for typing, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Let's start with something small. 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read the meaning next to it. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to look at the word while you listen, so your eyes and ears learn it together. 2. Now say the word out loud. Say it with me, slowly. Then say the meaning in your own words, not the same words as the page. For example, for Grow you might say "it gets bigger". A good try is your own words, even if they are simple. 3. Next, type a sentence with that word in the box, and press Check sentence. A good sentence uses the word the right way and says something real, like "My goat can grow bigger." Then read what the checker says to you. If it asks you to fix something, change your sentence and press Check sentence again. 4. Now do the same three things for every word on the page: press Listen, say the word and the meaning out loud, then type a sentence and press Check sentence. Take your time — there's no rush. Do one word, then the next. I expect one sentence from you for each word. 5. When every word has a sentence, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the science words. Only press it when you have really done them all. That button tells the page you finished this part. 6. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same words. Press Start on the first slide. This is like practising the words again, but one at a time on a card. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: press Listen, say the word and its meaning out loud, then type your sentence and press Check sentence. You can make a NEW sentence here if you want — that is even better practice. 8. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are, and how many slides are left. 9. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That finishes the slide deck. You will know the whole page is done when two things are true: you pressed I explored the science words at the bottom of the page, and you pressed the finish button on the last slide. Come back and tell me when you finish, and tell me which word was the trickiest. I will help you with that one. 🌱

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a walk. It shows you what Unit 1, Being Alive, is all about. By the end of this page you will know what you are going to learn: which things are living, and what living things need. You need only two things: your eyes to read, and your voice to talk. A grown-up can sit with you and help you read. Here is what I expect from you. Read slowly. Look at every word. Then tell me in your own words what you think you will learn. There are 3 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview on your screen. It tells you what this unit is about and what you will be able to do at the end. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and hear the words read out loud. Read with your finger under the words if that helps. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect you to read the whole box, not just the first line. Step 2. Now close your mouth for a moment and think. Then say out loud what you think you will learn in this unit. Say it to your grown-up, or say it to me here in the chat. A good answer sounds like this: "I will learn which things are alive and which things are not alive." One or two sentences is plenty. I expect your own words, not copied words — that is how I know it is really in your head. Step 3. When you have said your sentence, press Continue. That button takes you to The Lesson, where we start learning properly. Do not press Continue before you have talked about step 2. Pressing the button is your job, not mine. You will know this page is finished when you have read the overview, said your own sentence out loud, and pressed Continue and the next page opens. Now go and do step 1. Tell me when you have read it, and I will listen to your sentence. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Visual Models. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes of our big ideas. They help you SEE what "living" and "not living" mean. By the end you will be able to look at a model and say why something is alive. All you need is your eyes, your finger on the screen, and your voice. Here is what I expect from you. Look slowly. Say what you see out loud. Use our science words: living, non-living, animal, plant, grow. There are 4 models and 3 things to do. Here are all the steps. Step 1: Look at the first model, "Living or Not Living?". Look at it for a slow count of five. If it moves, drag it with your finger to turn it around. Press its buttons to change it. Then say out loud one thing you notice. Step 2: Look at the second model, "What Living Things Need". Drag it and press its buttons again. As you look, try to name the four needs: food, water, air and warmth. I expect you to say all four, even if you need a peek at the caption. Step 3: Look at the third model, "Animals and Plants Are Alive". Turn it and press its buttons. Then tell yourself three signs a plant is alive: it grows, it drinks water, it makes food in the sun. Step 4: Look at the fourth model, "Caring for Living Things". Turn it and press its buttons. Then think of one living thing at your home that you can care for today. Step 5: Under each model there is a caption. That is the little bit of writing. Read it, then press Listen to hear it. Listen right to the end, quietly, so you catch every word. Step 6: Go back to any model that felt tricky. Look one more time and listen again. Good scientists look twice! Step 7: When you have looked at all 4 models and heard all 4 captions, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models. Press it yourself — I cannot press it for you. Now start with Step 1. Tell me one thing you notice in the first model, and I will be right here. 🌱

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
# Our Explore the Concept Lesson

Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are going to be science detectives. 🔍

This page has 4 discoveries about living things. A discovery is a little puzzle. You look, you think, and you tell me your idea. By the end, you will be able to say if something is living or not living — and say WHY. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your typing finger. Let's find out. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3 and 4. Press the tab that says 1. A situation will open, with a picture or a model to look at. Look at the picture slowly. I expect you to really LOOK, not rush. Ask yourself in your head: does this thing eat? Does it drink? Does it grow? Can it have babies? Step 2. Now read the discovery question under the picture. Read it twice. Then think for a moment before you type. There is no rush. Step 3. Type your idea in the box. Try to write WHY, not just yes or no. A good answer sounds like this: "It is living because it grows and drinks water." The word "because" is your magic word — I want to see it in your answer! Step 4. Press the button that says Check my idea. If it says Exactly!, well done — the tab gets a little tick. If it says Look again, that is okay. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 5. If you got Look again, press the button that says Hint. Read the hint carefully. It will point you at the right idea. Then change your answer a little bit and press Check my idea one more time. Step 6. Now press tab 2, and do the very same thing: look, read, think, type your idea, press Check my idea. Then do tab 3. Then do tab 4. Do them one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 7. When all 4 tabs have a tick, the top part of the page is done. That is how you know: four discoveries, four ticks. Brilliant! Step 8. Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides there. The slides have the same discoveries, one discovery on each slide. On the first slide, press the button that says Start. Step 9. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. You are an expert at these buttons now! Step 10. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on. Keep going until you reach the last slide. Step 11. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished all your work. How you will know the page is finished: all 4 tabs have a tick, AND you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are all done! Now, off you go — press tab 1 and tell me what you see. I'm right here. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Let's learn the method together today. This page shows you 4 methods. A method is a way to do something, step by step, like a recipe. Ours are about living things: Watch a Seed Grow, the Living or Not Living Hunt, A Plant Needs Water, and Caring for Living Things. We do this so you learn how scientists work — look carefully, then say what you saw. By the end you will know the steps of all 4 methods. You need your eyes, your reading voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. Here is what I expect from you: read each step, say it out loud, and think "what would I do here?" Slow and careful is better than fast. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step. Say it out loud in your own voice. Then press Show me the next step. I expect you to say the words out loud, not just in your head — that helps your brain remember. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step. Read each new step out loud too. Keep going until the page says Method complete. When you see Method complete, that method is done. Well done! 3. Now do the very same thing for every method — all 4 of them. Read a step, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, and stop when it says Method complete. When all 4 say Method complete, the top part of the page is finished. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same methods. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on that slide to move through the steps, saying each one out loud. 5. When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are. Do every slide the same way: press Start, step through, then arrow to the next. 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. You will know the page is finished when all 4 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step 1, and tell me when your first method says Method complete. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a question with the answer already worked out for you. We use them so you can see HOW a good scientist thinks, not just what the answer is. Every example on this page is about our big idea: living things grow, eat, drink and can have young. By the end, you will be able to look at a thing and say if it is living or not living, and say why. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if you want to say your answers out loud. Here is what I expect from you: try each question in your head FIRST, before you peek. Say your answer with a "because". Not just "living" — say "living, because it eats and grows." That "because" is the science part! Step 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question slowly, twice. Do not press anything yet. Say your own answer out loud, with a because. Even if you are not sure, guess — guessing is fine here, and mistakes are how we learn. Step 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read the working line by line and compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I say the same thing? Did I remember my because? If you got it, say "yes!" If you did not, that is good too — now you know something new. Step 3. Do the same for all 8 examples: read, think, then press Show worked solution. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It counts how many you have opened. Keep going until the counter shows all 8. Step 4. Watch out for the tricky ones. A toy car moves, but it is NOT living, because it does not eat, drink or grow. A mango tree does not walk, but it IS living, because it grows, drinks water and makes new seeds. Moving is not the test! Step 5. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: read the question, think of your answer with a because, then press Show worked solution to check. Step 7. When you have finished a slide, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. Step 8. On the very last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 8 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Go and do Step 1, then come back and tell me your answer for example one — with your because! 🌱

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Guided Practice page. Guided Practice means we practise together. You have 12 short questions about living and non-living things. They help you remember the big idea: living things grow, eat, drink, need air and warmth, and can have young. Non-living things do none of these. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. Take your time — there is no rush. Here is what I expect from you. Try each question yourself first. Say your answer in a full sentence with a "because" in it, like "It is living because it grows." And if you get one wrong, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Now here are all the steps. Step 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Then ask the four questions in your head: Does it grow? Does it eat? Does it drink? Can it have babies? Work it out on paper or in your head before you type anything. I expect you to think first, not guess first. Step 2. Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Write a little sentence, not just one word. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step — that shows you one line of the working. Using a hint is smart, not cheating. I expect you to try once before you press hint. Step 3. Do this for every one of the 12 questions, until each one is right. If your answer is not right, read the feedback, think again, and try once more. I expect you to fix wrong answers yourself, with a hint if you need one. When all 12 are right, that part is finished. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Answer that slide, using the same buttons: Check my answer, Give me a hint, Show next step. This is your second go, so it should feel easier. Step 5. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are — they help you see how many are left. Do one slide at a time. I expect you to say your answer out loud before you type it, so your mouth and your brain agree! Step 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? All 12 questions are marked right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you have completed Guided Practice. Ready? Tell me the first question when you have read it, and we will look at that together. 🌱

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. This page is called Quick Reference. It is like a little box that holds all the big words and facts of Unit 1: Being Alive. We come here to remember what we learned, so the ideas stay in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what "living" means, what "non-living" means, and the four things living things need. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. There are three steps. Step 1: Read the Quick Reference. Look at the words on the page, one at a time, slowly. Where you see a small speaker, press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Try to say each word after the voice. I expect you to read all the way down, not just the first line, and to stop on any word that feels tricky. Step 2: Say the key facts in your own words. Now close your eyes for a moment and say it out loud, like you are teaching a friend. A good answer sounds like this: "Living things grow, eat, drink, breathe air, and can have babies. Non-living things never do those things." Then say the four needs: food, water, air and warmth. I expect your own words, not copied words. Say them out loud, even if a grown-up is listening. Step 3: Press Reference reviewed. Go to the bottom of the page and press the button that says Reference reviewed. Only press it after you have really read the page and said the facts out loud. That button tells the page you are done, and I cannot press it for you. You will know the page is finished when you have read every word, said the key facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Now go and do Step 1. Tell me when you have read the page, and tell me one word that felt tricky. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text:
Hello, my scientist! Today we are on the Experiments page of Unit 1, Being Alive. This page has six hands-on experiments. You will look at real things, sort them, water a plant, watch a seed, and find baby animals. By the end you will be able to say which things are living and which things are not living, and why. You need a pencil, a grown-up nearby to help you find things, and your good looking eyes. Here is the whole page, step by step. There are seven steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the first experiment box on the page. Press Listen and listen to the words. Then read them again with your eyes. Each box tells you what to use and what to do. I expect you to know two things before you move: what things you need, and what you must look at. Step 2. Go and get the things it names. They are easy home things, like a seed, a cup, water, a stone, a spoon, a leaf. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. I expect you to have everything on the table before you start, like a real scientist. Step 3. Before you begin, make a prediction. A prediction means what you think will happen. Say it out loud, like "I think the seed will grow." Scientists ask questions exactly like that one. I expect one clear guess from you, and it is fine if your guess turns out wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 4. Now do the activity. Go slowly and watch carefully. Ask yourself the four living questions: Does it grow? Does it eat? Does it drink? Can it have babies? I expect you to look for a whole minute before you decide. Step 5. Write your answer in the box under the activity. Write what you saw, not just yes or no. A good answer uses our science words, like living, non-living, animal, plant, grow. For example you might write: the stone is non-living because it does not eat or grow. I expect one sentence with a because in it. Step 6. Press Mark complete under that activity. Then do the same for the next experiment box: Listen, get the things, predict, do it, write it, Mark complete. Keep going until all six are marked. When every one is marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same experiments, one experiment on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide, just like you did above. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when all six boxes say complete, you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom of the page, and the last slide is done too. I do not tick anything for you — you press the buttons, because the work is yours. 🌱

When you are ready, tell me which experiment you are starting with, and I will help you with that one.

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Science Fluency. Let me tell you what it is and why we do it. Science Fluency is a quick sprint of 12 short questions about living and not living things. We do it so the big idea gets fast in your head — you should not have to think for a long time to know that a goat is living and a spoon is not. All you need is your reading eyes, your fingers to type, and your brain warmed up. There are a few simple steps, and I will walk you through every one. Step 1: Get ready before you start. Say the four living tests out loud to yourself: does it grow, does it eat, does it drink, can it have babies? Then say the four needs: food, water, air, warmth. I expect you to say these out loud, not just think them — that is what makes you fast. Step 2: Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. That is just to help you go quickly. Do not worry about it. Take your time — there's no rush, but try not to stop and stare. Step 3: Read question one. Read it twice. Ask yourself the four tests. Then type your answer in the answer box. Step 4: Make your answer a good one. A good answer says WHAT it is and WHY. Not just "living" — say "living, because it eats and grows". That is what I expect from you every time. Step 5: Press Check & continue. This checks your answer and takes you to the next question. Press it once for each question. Step 6: Keep going, one question at a time, until you have done all 12. If a question feels hard, do not stop. Give your best answer and press Check & continue. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 7: Watch out for the tricky ones. A toy car moves, but moving is not the test — a toy car does not eat or grow, so it is not living. A mango tree does not walk, but it grows and drinks water, so it IS living. Remember these two and you will get lots right. Step 8: When the sprint ends, look at your score. You need most of them right. If you got enough right, well done — you are finished! Step 9: If you got fewer right than you needed, press Run the sprint again. This is not a bad thing. It just means one more go. Tell me which questions were hard first, and we will fix them together before you run it again. Step 10: The page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers. The page will show you that. I do not tick it for you — you finish it by pressing the buttons yourself. Now go and read question one. Tell me your answer and I will check it with you. Here comes question one.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Unit 1 games. This is our Being Alive unit, all about living and non-living things. Games help our brains remember. Each game asks you a small question. You pick the right answer and you win a star. By the end, you will be quick at saying what is living and what is not living. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and a comfy seat. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the games on your screen. Pick any one you like. Press Start game. A question will pop up with some answers to choose from. Read the question twice, then press the answer you think is right. If you get it right, you win a star! If you need help, press the clue. I expect you to think for a moment before you press — a slow good answer beats a fast guess. Step 2. When a game ends, press Play again. This gives you more chances to win stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. So keep playing that same game until every star is filled in. I expect you to try again with a smile, even if you get one wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Pick the next game, press Start game, answer the rounds, then press Play again until it has all its stars. Go game by game until none are left. I expect you to finish one game fully before you start a new one. How will you know the page is finished? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. You do not press anything special — it just knows you are done! One little tip from me: if a question asks "is it living?", ask yourself these four questions. Does it grow? Does it eat? Does it drink? Can it have babies? That trick will help you win lots of stars. Ready? Press Start game on your first game, and tell me how it goes!

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher for this page. This page is called Solve Real Problems. Here you use what you know about living things in real life stories — a hen, a plant, a hungry tummy. We do this because knowing a fact is good, but using it is even better. By the end you will be able to look at anything and say if it is living or not living, and say why. You need your eyes, your thinking, and the typing box on the screen. Let's start! 1. There are 6 problems on this page. Read the first one slowly. Then read it one more time. Ask yourself: what is this question really asking me? Is it asking "living or not living", or is it asking "what does it need", or is it asking "how can I be kind to it"? I expect you to know what the question wants before you type anything. 2. Now think of the answer in your head. Use your four helper questions: Does it grow? Does it eat? Does it drink? Can it have babies? And remember the four needs: food, water, air and warmth. I expect a "because" in your answer, like "the hen is living because…". The because part is the science part. 3. Type your answer in the box. Write your thinking too, not just one word. A good Grade 1 answer is one full sentence, with the word because in it. Then press Check answer. If your grown-up helps you spell, that is fine — the thinking must be yours. 4. If your brain feels stuck, do not worry. Press Hint. The hint gives you a little push, not the answer. Read it, think again, then type. Getting stuck and trying again is real science. 5. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Move on to the next one and do the same three things: read twice, think with your four questions, type and press Check answer. Do this for all 6 problems. The page is finished when every one of the 6 says it is right. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. This is your practice round. Press Start on the first slide. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need help. I expect you to say your answer out loud first, then type it. Saying it out loud helps it stick in your head. 8. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Take your time — there's no rush. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? All 6 problems will say your answer is right, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide. 🌱

Ready? Read problem number one and tell me what you think it is asking. I am right here with you.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Explain Your Thinking page. On this page you say WHY you think something. That is what scientists do — they give a reason. It will help you remember our big idea: living things grow, eat, drink, and can have babies. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your words. There are four steps, and I will give you all four now. Step 1. Look at the page. You will see 4 questions. They are called prompts. Read the first one slowly. Under it you will see some key ideas — these are the special science words you should use, like living, non-living, animal, plant. I expect you to read the prompt twice and say out loud, "I know this one is..." before you write. Step 2. Now write in the box. Say three things: what you see, which rule you used, and your answer. A good answer sounds like this: "It grows, it drinks water, so it is living." When you are done, press Check scientific ideas. If the page asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check scientific ideas again. I expect a full sentence, not just one word. Step 3. Now press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Look for the key ideas in it. Ask yourself: did I use those words too? If you missed one, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for all 4 prompts. Step 4. Look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons you already know on each slide. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know you are done? Every prompt has your own explanation, every one used the key ideas, and you pressed the finish button on the last slide. 🌱

Ready? Tell me when you have read prompt one, and we will do it together.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today we learn about Growing Plants. This page is called The Lesson. It has three short ideas about plants: the parts of a plant, what plants need, and how a seed grows. By the end you will be able to name the parts of a plant and say what each one does. You need your eyes, your voice, and a plant near you if there is one. Let's start! 1. Look at the first concept box. Read it slowly, word by word. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. Listening helps the words stick. I expect you to read and listen to all three concepts, one at a time, not in a hurry. 2. Each concept has an example at the end. Say that example out loud, with your own voice. Then try it for real. For the plant parts, point at a real plant and say: roots, stem, leaves, flower. Do this for each of the three concepts. 3. When you have read all three concepts and said all three examples, go to the bottom of the page. Press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you truly read them all. That button tells your teacher you are done. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. The same three ideas are there, one idea on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. 5. On each slide, use the same buttons you used before. Read the slide, listen if you can, and say the idea out loud in your own words. Try this: "Roots drink water." That is a good answer. 6. When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right. That takes you to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are in the deck. 7. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that is the end of the deck. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when step 1 is done, and I will check with you. 🌱

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 2: Growing Plants. This page is the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It tells you what we will learn and what you will be able to do at the end. You do not need a pencil yet — just your eyes, your ears, and your voice. There are 3 small steps. Here they are. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on your screen and read them slowly. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and hear the words too. Listen for the plant parts: roots, stem, leaves and flower. I expect you to read or listen all the way to the end, not just the first line. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud to your grown-up, or type it to me. A good answer has one or two things in it, like "I will learn the parts of a plant" or "I will learn what plants need to grow." I expect your own words, not the same words from the screen. Even a short answer is a good answer. Step 3: Press Continue to go to The Lesson. When you have read the page and said your idea, find the Continue button and press it. That takes you to the next part, where we learn together. I expect you to press it only after Step 1 and Step 2 are done. You will know the page is finished when you have read the overview, said what you will learn, and pressed Continue. Now go and do Step 1. Read the Unit Overview, and press Listen if you see the speaker. Tell me when you are done. 🌱

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Hello! Today we are on the Science Words page. These are the words we use when we talk about plants: roots, stem, leaves, flower, water, light, warmth and soil. We learn them so you can say what each plant part does, not just point at it. By the end you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You will need your voice, your eyes on the screen, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. Here is our plan. There are four parts. Take your time — there's no rush. 1. Start at the first word. Read the word and read what it means. Then press Listen to hear it said out loud. Listen carefully, and look at the word while you hear it. I expect you to do this for every word on the page, one at a time, from the top. 2. Now it is your turn to talk. Say the word out loud, nice and clear. Then say the meaning in YOUR own words, not the page's words. For example, for roots you might say "they drink water under the ground". Then type one sentence using the word and press Check sentence. Read what the checker tells you. A good sentence has the word in it and shows you know its job, like "The roots hold my bean plant in the soil." Do this for each word before you move on. 3. When you have done every word, scroll to the bottom and press I explored the science words. Only press it when you really have finished them all — that button tells the page you are done. 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: Listen, then say the word and the meaning, then your sentence and Check sentence. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when the I explored the science words button is pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide, and no dots are left to visit. Ready? Start with the first word, press Listen, and tell me which word it was.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. Here we look closely at plants, like real scientists do. You will find the parts of a plant — roots, stem, leaves and flower. You will also think about what a plant needs to grow. By the end, you will be able to name the plant parts and say what each one does. What you need: your eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. Take your time — there's no rush. What I expect from you: type your own idea, even a short one. Use plant words like roots, stem, leaves, flower, water and light. Guessing is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see four numbered tabs. Press tab number 1. Read the little story on the tab, and look at the picture or model with it. Look slowly, like you are watching a bird. I expect you to notice at least one thing in the picture before you move on. Step 2. Now read the discovery question on that tab. Think first. Then type your idea in the box and press Check my idea. A good answer uses a plant word — for example "the roots drink water". One short sentence is enough for me. Step 3. If the page says Look again, do not worry. Press Hint, read it, and try once more. The hint tells you where to look. I expect you to try again yourself before asking me — but if you are stuck, tell me and I will give you a small hint too. Step 4. When the page says Exactly!, that tab gets a tick. Well done! Now press tab number 2 and do the same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Then do tab 3, then tab 4, one at a time. Step 5. The page is done when all four discovery questions are answered right and every tab has a tick. Check the tabs and count the ticks with your finger: one, two, three, four. Step 6. Now scroll down under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 8. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done — I cannot press it for you. You will know the whole page is finished when every tab has a tick and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Go and press tab number 1, then come back and tell me what you see in the picture. 🌱

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello, my lovely learner! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes that show our plant ideas. Looking closely is real science work. By the end, you will be able to point to the parts of a plant, say what a plant needs, and tell how a seed grows. You need your eyes, your finger for dragging, and your voice for saying the words out loud. Step 1. Look at the first model, The Parts of a Plant. Put your finger on it and drag it slowly to turn it around. If it has buttons, press them one at a time and watch what changes. I want you to find four parts and say them out loud: roots, stem, leaves, flower. Step 2. Look at the second model, What Plants Need to Grow. Drag it and press its buttons too. Look for the sun, the water, the warm air and the soil. I want you to name all four things a plant needs: water, light, warmth and soil. Step 3. Look at the third model, Planting a Seed. Drag it and press its buttons to see the seed change. Watch which part comes out of the seed first. I want you to tell me this: does the root go down first, or does the shoot go up first? Step 4. Now read the caption under each model. A caption is the little bit of writing that tells you about the picture. Read it slowly, word by word. Step 5. Press Listen under each caption. Listen carefully to the whole thing. Then say one new word back to me, like roots or soil. Step 6. When you have looked at all three models and listened to all three captions, press the button that says I explored the models at the bottom of the page. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models. Take your time — there is no rush. Tell me when you finish Step 1, and I will cheer you on! 🌱

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are working on the Worked Examples page for Growing Plants. A worked example is a question with the answer already shown, step by step. It is like watching me solve it, then trying it yourself. We do this so plant words like roots, stem, leaves and flower become easy for you. By the end you will be able to say each plant part and its job. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want to say your answers out loud. Here are the steps. There are 8 examples on the page, then some slides at the bottom. 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question first, before you look at anything else. Say your own answer out loud, even if you are not sure. I expect a guess from you every time — a guess is good thinking, not a mistake. 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read the answer slowly. Compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I say the same thing? Did I use the right plant word? 3. If your answer matched, say "I got it!" and smile. If it did not match, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the answer one more time, then say it in your own words. 4. Do the same for every one of the 8 examples. Read the question, say your answer, then press Show worked solution. Take your time — there's no rush. 5. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It counts how many examples you have opened. Keep going until it shows all 8. The page wants every single one opened. 6. Now go under the page. There is a deck of slides there. Each slide has one of the same examples on it. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 7. On each slide, do the same thing as before: read the question, say your answer, then press the button to show the solution. One slide at a time. 8. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. More dots filled means you are getting close to the end. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 8 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with example one, and tell me what you think the answer is. I'm right here with you.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Welcome to Guided Practice! This is where we practise everything we learned about growing plants. You will answer questions about roots, stem, leaves and flower, and about what plants need. Why do we do it? Because practice makes the words stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to name the plant parts and say what each one does. What you need: your pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. What I expect from you: try your own answer first, before any hint. Use the plant words when you write. And it is okay to get one wrong — mistakes are how we learn. Here are all the steps. Do them one at a time, slowly. 1. Read the first question. There are 12 questions on this page. Read it twice, out loud if you can. Then work out your answer on paper or in your head. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Write a short, clear answer, like "the roots" or "the leaves". I expect a real try from you, not a guess like "I don't know". 3. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can press it up to three times, and each hint tells you a bit more. Try again after each hint before you press it again. 4. If the hints are not enough, press Show next step. That shows you one line of the working. Read it, then finish the answer yourself. The answer still needs to come from you — I'll help you get there. 5. Do this for every question, one by one, until each one is right. If one is wrong, read it again and fix it. Green ticks all the way down means you did it. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. 7. On each slide, use the same buttons: type your answer and press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. Say the plant word out loud too — that helps you remember it. 8. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many are left. 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. Well done — that is the end of the slides. How will you know the page is finished? When all 12 questions are answered right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Remember to press the buttons yourself, because that is how the page saves your good work. Ready? Tell me question one, and let's do it together.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Learn the Method page. Well done for getting here. A method is a way to do something step by step, like a little recipe. This page has 4 methods about growing plants. We do this so you learn the right order to work, and so you can name the plant parts: roots, stem, leaves and flower. Here is what I expect from you. Say each step out loud in your own voice. Go slowly, one step at a time. Do not rush to the end. If a step feels hard, tell me and I will help. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. A pencil is nice too, for drawing a plant later. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Say it out loud. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. A good job here is speaking clearly and understanding what the step asks you to do. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step, again and again. Say every new step out loud before you press. Stop when the page tells you Method complete. That means you finished that method all the way to the end. 3. Now do the very same thing for every method. There are 4 in all. Press Show me the next step until each one says Method complete. Take your time with each one. I expect all 4 to be finished, not just the first. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides, with the same methods, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons to move through the steps. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 4 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Tell me when you have pressed Start on the first method, and I will stay right here with you. 🌱

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today we are on the Quick Reference page. This page is like a little card that holds all the big ideas of our plant unit in one place. We do this so the words stay warm in your head, ready for later. You will need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. Here are our three steps. Step 1: Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page slowly, from the top to the bottom. It shows our plant words like roots, stem, leaves and flower, and what each one means. Where you see a speaker button, press Listen and hear the word said out loud. I expect you to go slowly, not fast — read one word, then stop and picture it in a real plant. Step 2: Say the key facts in your own words. Now close your eyes for a second and say them out loud, like you are teaching a friend. Try this: "Roots drink water. The stem holds the plant up. Leaves catch the sunlight. The flower makes new seeds." Then add what a plant needs: water, light, warmth and soil. I expect your own words, not the page's words — that is how I know you really understand. Step 3: Press Reference reviewed. This button is at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you have read everything and said the facts out loud. I expect you to be honest with yourself — if a word still feels fuzzy, go back and read it again first. You will know the page is finished when you have read it, said the facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed at the bottom. Now start with Step 1. Read slowly, and press Listen where you see a speaker. Tell me when you are done, and I will listen to your own words. 🌱

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text: Hello, scientist! Today we are doing our Experiments page for Growing Plants. Real scientists learn by looking and trying, and that is what you will do. You will grow a bean, plant a seed, and find out what plants need. By the end you will be able to name the parts of a plant and say what helps it grow. You will need a grown-up nearby, a pencil, and some simple things from home like a cup, soil, water and a bean. Here are all the steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Look at the first experiment on the page. Read what it says, and press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listening while you read helps the words stick. Then go and get the things it names, like a cup, a bean, or a little water. I expect you to have everything ready before you start, like a real scientist setting up a lab. Step 2: Before you begin, make a prediction. That means you guess what will happen. Say it out loud to your grown-up, like "I think the root will come out first." Scientists ask questions exactly like that one, and a guess is never wrong — it is just a guess. Step 3: Now do the activity. Go slowly and look carefully with your eyes. Notice colours, sizes and any changes. Some experiments take a few days, so you may need to look again tomorrow. That is fine — plants grow slowly! Step 4: Write your answer, or what you noticed, in the box on the page. Try to use our science words: roots, stem, leaves, flower, water, light, warmth, soil. A good answer says what you saw, not just "it was nice." For example, "The root grew down first." One or two sentences is plenty for Grade 1. Step 5: When that experiment is done and your box is filled in, press Mark complete under it. That button tells the page you finished it. I expect you to press it only after you really did the activity and wrote something — that is honest scientist work. Step 6: Now do the same for all 6 experiments, one at a time. Read and press Listen, get your things, predict, do it, write in the box, then press Mark complete. Do not rush ahead — finish one before you start the next. Step 7: When every experiment has Mark complete pressed, scroll to the bottom and press Finish activities. That saves your good work. Well done — that is the top part of the page done! Step 8: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same experiments, one experiment on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. Step 9: On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: Listen, then write in the box, then Mark complete. You know how to do this now, so it should feel easy. Step 10: Press the arrow on the right side to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going until you reach the last slide. Step 11: On the last slide, press Finish activities. That is the end! You will know the whole page is finished when every experiment says complete, and you have pressed Finish activities twice — once at the bottom of the page, and once on the last slide. Ready to start Step 1? Tell me which experiment is first on your screen, and I will help you get set up. 🌱

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Games on our Growing Plants page. These games ask you quick questions about plants. Roots, stem, leaves, flower, water, light, warmth and soil — all our unit words. Playing helps the words stick in your head, so you remember them without even trying. You will need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a grown-up sitting close by. Here is what I expect from you: read each question slowly, think before you tap, and keep going even if one is tricky. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1. Pick one game on the page and press Start game. A question will pop up with four choices. Read the question twice, then tap the answer you think is right. If you get it right, you earn a star! If not, read the little explanation — it tells you the right answer, and that helps you next time. Keep answering until the rounds are done. I expect you to try every round, not skip any. Step 2. When the game ends, press Play again. You will see the questions again, and you can win more stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. So play that same game again and again until its stars are full. I expect you to stay with one game until it is mastered, before you move on. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3. Now do the same with every game on the page. Choose the next game, press Start game, answer the rounds, then press Play again until all its stars are full. Work through them one by one until every game is mastered. I expect you to use our plant words while you play — say them out loud, like "roots drink water" or "leaves catch sunlight". You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars. The page finishes by itself then — you do not press anything extra. Ready? Press Start game on your first game, and tell me how it goes! 🌱

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today we are on the page called Solve Real Problems. Here you use what you know about plants in real life — at home, at the market, outside in nature. There are 6 little problems to think about. By the end you will be able to look at a real plant problem and say what is happening and why. You need your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Let's begin! What I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then answer in your own words. Use our plant words when you can: roots, stem, leaves, flower, water, light, warmth, soil. Good try beats fast try. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Read the first problem carefully. Read it twice, not once. Ask yourself: what is this question really asking me? Is it asking for a plant part? Or what a plant needs? Point at the words with your finger as you read. I expect you to know what the question wants before you write anything. Step 2: Now think of your answer, then type it in the box and press Check answer. Write a short sentence, not just one word. For example, say the part AND its job, like "the roots, because they drink water." If you feel stuck, press Hint first and read it — the hint gives you a little nudge, not the answer. Then try again yourself. Step 3: When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done — go on to the next problem and do the same thing again: read twice, think, type, press Check answer. Keep going until all 6 problems say you are right. If one says not quite, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again and look for the small thing you missed. Step 4: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. This is your practice round, so try to answer without peeking back. Step 5: On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint if you need a little help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on and how many are left. Step 6: On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have finished all your work. I expect you to press it yourself, because it saves what you did. How you will know the page is finished: all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Tell me when you have read problem number one, and tell me what you think it is asking. I'm right here with you. 🌱

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Science Fluency page. Let me tell you what it is. This is a sprint. That means 12 quick questions about growing plants. You answer as fast as you can, but carefully too. We do this so the plant words become easy for you — roots, stem, leaves, flower, water, light, warmth, soil. By the end, you will be able to say what each plant part does without stopping to think. What I expect from you: try every question yourself first, write a short clear answer, and use the plant words. Short is fine! "The roots" is a great answer. If you get stuck, ask me and I will give you a hint, not the answer. Here are your steps, one at a time. 1. Get ready. Sit up and have a quick look at the top of the page — there is a timer there. It counts your time. Do not worry about it. Fast is nice, but right is better. 2. Read question one. Read it twice, slowly. Ask yourself: is it asking about a plant part, or about what a plant needs? 3. Type your answer in the box. Use a plant word if you can. For example, if a question asks about a part under the soil, your answer should name that part. 4. Press Check & continue. This checks your answer and brings the next question. Press it once and wait a moment. 5. Look at what it tells you. If you were right, say a quiet "yes!" and keep going. If not, read the correct answer once and say it out loud. That helps your brain keep it. 6. Do the same for every question, all the way to question twelve. Read, type, press Check & continue. One question at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. 7. If a question feels too hard, do not stop the sprint. Make your best guess, press Check & continue, and remember that question. You can ask me about it after. 8. When question twelve is done, the page shows your score. Look at how many you got right out of 12. 9. If you got most of them right, well done — you have finished! If you got fewer, press Run the sprint again. That is not a bad thing at all. Mistakes are how we learn. 10. Before you run it again, come and tell me which questions were tricky. We will practise just those together, then you try the sprint once more. You will know the page is finished when you complete a whole sprint with enough answers right — the page will show that you passed. Then you can smile, because you did it. Ready? Start with step one, and tell me when question one is on your screen. 🌱

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today you are the science explainer. This page is called Explain Your Thinking. Instead of picking one answer, you tell me HOW you know. That is what real scientists do. You will need your reading eyes, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. What I expect from you: use our plant words — roots, stem, leaves, flower, water, light, warmth, soil. Try your own words first, before you peek at any model answer. Good thinking! Step 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. Read it slowly, twice. Under the prompt you will see the key ideas. Those are the words I want to hear in your answer. Step 2. Click inside the answer box and write your explanation. Say what you know, then say why. A good answer sounds like this: "I think this because a plant needs light, and light comes from the sun." Two or three sentences is plenty for you. Step 3. Press the button that says Check scientific ideas. If the page says you need more, do not worry. Add one more sentence with a key idea word, then press Check scientific ideas again. Step 4. Now press Show model explanation. Read it and compare. Ask yourself: did I use the same science words? You do not have to copy it. It is only there to help you see a strong answer. Step 5. Do the same three things for prompt two, prompt three and prompt four. There are 4 prompts in all. Read, write, press Check scientific ideas, then peek at Show model explanation. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7. On each slide, do exactly what you did above: write your explanation, press Check scientific ideas, then press Show model explanation. Say your answer out loud too. That helps it stick. Step 8. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Keep going until the dots run out. Step 9. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when all 4 prompts have your own explanation, every one uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read prompt one and tell me what it is asking. 🌱

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 3. It is called "Ourselves". This unit is all about YOU — your body, your face, and your five senses. This first page is our little map. It shows what we will learn together. You only need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Here are the three things to do, one at a time. 1. Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page and read them slowly. If you see a small speaker, press Listen and let it read to you. Listening and looking at the same time helps a lot. I expect you to read every line, not just the first one. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Say what you think you will learn. Now close your mouth for a second and think. Then say it out loud, in your own words. You can say it to a grown-up near you, or just to yourself. A good answer sounds like this: "I will learn my body parts and my five senses." One or two sentences is plenty. I expect real words from you, out loud — not just in your head. 3. Press Continue to go to The Lesson. Find the button that says Continue and press it. Only press it after you have read the page and said your sentence. That button takes you to our first lesson. You will know this page is finished when you have read it all, said your own sentence out loud, and pressed Continue. Then the next page opens for us. Great start! Come and tell me your sentence when you have said it — I would love to hear it. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our lesson page for Unit 3: Ourselves. This page has four small lessons, called concepts. They teach you the parts of your body, how people are the same and different, the five senses, and how to stay clean and healthy. We do this so you can point to your own body parts and name them, and say which part sees, hears, smells, tastes and feels. Here is what I expect from you: sit up, use your own body to try each part, say the words out loud, and take your time. You need your voice, your hands, and a grown-up nearby if you want help. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Read the first concept slowly, then press Listen to hear it read to you. Follow along with the words while you listen. Do this for all four concepts, one at a time. I expect you to read every one, not skip any. Step 2: At the end of each concept there is an example. Say it out loud, then do it with your own body. Touch your head and say "head". Touch your arms, hands, legs and feet and say each name. Count your fingers: one, two, three, all the way to ten. I expect to hear your voice saying the words, not just your eyes reading them. Step 3: When you have read all four concepts and tried all four examples, go to the bottom of the page and press the button that says I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really did read them all. That button tells the page you finished your reading. Step 4: Under the page there is a deck of slides. They show the same four concepts, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide, then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts, and the last slide is done with the finish button pressed. Ready? Start with Step 1 now, and tell me when the first concept is read. Then I will check in with you. 🙂

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. Here is what it is. You will meet four little discoveries about your body and your five senses. You will look, think, and write your own idea. This helps you learn the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and your hands to type. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. Here is what I expect from you. Try your own idea first, even a small one. Use words like eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin. Do not worry about a wrong try. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1: Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3 and 4. Press tab number 1. Read the little story on it, and look at the picture or model. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect you to look carefully and notice one thing before you answer. Step 2: Now read the discovery question on that tab. Think quietly for a moment. Then type your idea in the box in your own words. A good answer names the body part, like "my ears" or "my nose". Then press Check my idea. Step 3: Look at what the page says back to you. If it says Look again, that is fine! Press Hint, read it, then try once more. When it says Exactly!, the tab gets a little tick. That tick means well done. Step 4: Now press tab number 2. Do the same three things: read, think, type your idea, press Check my idea. Then do tab 3, then tab 4, the same way. I expect all four tabs to have a tick. Step 5: Now scroll down to the bottom of the page. There is a deck of slides there. It has the same discoveries again, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 6: On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 7: Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? Every numbered tab has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is the whole page complete! Now go and press tab number 1. When you have read it, come back and tell me what you see. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes of the ideas in Unit 3, Ourselves. They show your body parts, how people are the same and different, your five senses, and how to stay clean and healthy. We look at them so the ideas go into your eyes and stick in your mind. You need your eyes, your finger to press and drag, and your voice to say the words out loud. There are 3 steps. Here they all are. Step 1. Look at all 4 models, one at a time. Start with the first model and look at the whole picture. If it moves, drag it with your finger or mouse to turn it around. Press any buttons on it to make it change, and watch what happens. I expect you to touch your own body while you look — touch your head, arms, legs, hands and feet, and say each word out loud. Do not rush. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Read the caption under each model, then press Listen. The caption is the little bit of writing under the picture. Read it first, then press Listen and hear it read to you. I expect you to say one thing you notice about each model, like "I see two eyes" or "hands hold things." Do this for all 4 models before you move on. Step 3. Press I explored the models at the bottom of the page. Only press it after you have looked at all 4 models and listened to all 4 captions. That button tells the page you are done. I cannot press it for you — the record of your work must come from you. You will know the page is finished when you have seen all 4 models, heard all 4 captions, and pressed I explored the models. Ready? Start with model 1 now, and tell me what you see. 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are working on the Worked Examples page for our unit, Ourselves. A worked example is a question with the answer already worked out for you. We use them so you can try first, then check if you thought the same way. By the end you will be able to name body parts and the five senses with confidence. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby to help you read. There are four things to do. Here they all are. Step 1: Look at the first worked example. Read the question out loud, slowly. Before you press anything, say your own answer out loud, like "I see with my eyes." I expect you to try first, even if you are not sure. A guess with good thinking is a great start. Step 2: Now press Show worked solution. Read the solution and compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I say the same body part? If you did, say "yes!" to yourself. If you did not, read the solution again and say it out loud once, so your brain remembers it. Step 3: Do the same for all 8 worked examples, one at a time. Read, say your answer, then press Show worked solution. At the top of the page there is a counter. It tells you how many you have opened. I expect you to keep going until the counter shows all 8. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 4: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Say your answer out loud, then use the same buttons on the slide to see the solution. Step 5: To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are in the deck. I expect you to answer out loud on every slide before you look, just like before. Step 6: On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 8 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with worked example one, and tell me your answer to it. I'm listening! 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Learn the Method page in our unit, Ourselves. A method is a way to do something step by step, like a little recipe. On this page there are 4 methods about our body and our senses. We do this so you learn how scientists work: look carefully, then say what you found. By the end you will be able to say the steps out loud all by yourself. You only need your eyes, your voice, and your finger to press the buttons. What I expect from you: press the buttons yourself, say every step out loud in a clear voice, and take your time. Reading in your head is good. Reading out loud is even better! Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step out loud. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. A new step will appear underneath. Do not rush — I want to hear each step said slowly and clearly. 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step again and again. Say each new step out loud as it appears. Keep going until the page says Method complete. When you see those words, that method is done. Well done — one finished! 3. Now do the very same thing for every method on the page. There are 4 in all. Go to the next method, read step one out loud, and press Show me the next step until it says Method complete. Then the next one, then the last one. This part of the page is finished when all 4 methods say Method complete. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same methods on it. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on the slide to move through the steps, saying each one out loud, just like before. 5. When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right side. That takes you to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Do the same thing on every slide: Start, then step through, then the arrow. 6. On the last slide, do the steps as usual, then press the finish button. Nice work — that closes the deck. How will you know the whole page is finished? Two things must be true. All 4 methods on the page say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Now go ahead and start with step 1. Tell me when your first method says Method complete, and I will check in with you. Take your time — there's no rush.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today we are on the Quick Reference page for Unit 3, "Ourselves". This page is like a little pocket of all our best facts. It has our body words, our five senses, and how we stay clean and healthy, all in one place. We do this so the words stay in your head and feel easy. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are three steps. Here they all are. 1. Read the Quick Reference. Look at the page from the top to the bottom. Read it slowly, one line at a time. Where you see a speaker button, press Listen and listen carefully. Then say the word out loud too. I expect you to read every word box, not just look at the pictures. If a word feels tricky, stop and say it three times. 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Now look away from the page for a moment. Tell me, or tell your grown-up, what you remember. Try to say the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Then say which body part goes with each one. I expect your own words, not the page's exact words. Saying "we see with our eyes" is perfect. If you forget one, peek at the page, then say it again without peeking. 3. Press Reference reviewed. When you have read the page and said the facts out loud, scroll to the bottom. Press the button that says Reference reviewed. Only press it after you really read, because that button is your promise that you did the work. I expect you to press it yourself. You will know the page is finished when you have read every part, said the five senses in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Then this page is complete. Let's start with step 1. Read the Quick Reference slowly and press Listen where you see a speaker. Tell me when you are done, and tell me one word that was new for you. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text:
Hello! I am your teacher for this page. Let us do some science with our own bodies! This page is called Experiments. There are 6 hands-on experiments. In each one you will use your senses — sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. We do this because senses are how your body learns about the world. By the end, you will be able to name body parts, name the five senses, and say which body part does each job. What you need: a pencil, a grown-up nearby to help, and a few safe things from home like a spoon, a cup, a soft sock and a piece of fruit. Never touch anything hot, and only taste food your grown-up gives you. What I expect from you: try each one for real, look and listen carefully, and write what you noticed in your own words. Even one true sentence is great work. Step 1. Read the first experiment. It tells you what to use and what to do. Press Listen to hear it read out loud. Listen once, then read it again with your eyes. Now go and get the things it names and put them on the table. I expect you to have the right things ready before you start. Step 2. Do the activity with your hands. Take your time — there's no rush. Then write in the box what you did and what you noticed. A good answer uses a science word from our unit, like eyes, ears, nose, mouth, hands or senses. For example: "I closed my eyes and I heard a tap. My ears told me."

Step 3. When that one is done, press Mark complete under it. Only press it after you really did the activity and wrote in the box. That button tells the page, "I finished this one."

Step 4. Now do the same for all 6 experiments, one at a time. Read, press Listen, get the things, do it, write in the box, press Mark complete. Do not rush ahead. One experiment, then the next. Step 5. When every experiment has Mark complete pressed, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. That saves all your good work. Step 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. It has the same experiments, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 7. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, then do it, then write your answer, then Mark complete. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 8. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Do every slide the same way, all the way to the last one. Step 9. On the last slide, press Finish activities. How will you know the page is done?
