Every experiment has Mark complete pressed, you pressed Finish activities on the page, and you pressed Finish activities on the last slide too. Ready to begin? Tell me when you have your things for the first experiment, and I will check in with you. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are on the Guided Practice page for our unit, Ourselves. This page has 12 short questions about your body and your five senses. We do it so the words stick in your head: eyes, ears, nose, mouth, hands, feet. By the end you will be able to name a body part and say which sense it gives you. All you need is your own body to point to, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here is what I expect from you: try your own answer first, before you press anything. Say it out loud, then type it. Short answers are fine, like "eyes" or "five senses". Mistakes are how we learn, so a wrong try is still good work. Here are the steps, one at a time. Step 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Then touch the body part you think the answer is, or count on your fingers. I expect you to have an answer in your head before you type. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Type your answer in the box. Then press Check my answer. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints, so press it again if you need more. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it will show you one line of the thinking. I expect you to try a hint before you use Show next step — the hint helps your brain do the work. Step 3. Now do the same for every question, all 12 of them. Read, think, type, press Check my answer. If an answer is not right, do not worry — read the hint, fix it, and press Check my answer again. Keep going until every question is right. That is when this part of the page is done. Step 4. Look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it the same way, with the same buttons: Check my answer, Give me a hint, Show next step. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? Every one of the 12 questions is marked right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then the page has your work saved — I cannot mark it for you, only you can, by pressing those buttons. Ready? Tell me the first question you see, and we will look at it together. 😊

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today we are doing Science Fluency. That means quick thinking about our bodies and our five senses. It is like a little race — you answer twelve short questions as fast as you can. We do this so the words come to your mind quickly, without stopping to think hard. By the end, you will know your body parts and senses really well! What you need: just you, your fingers to type, and maybe a grown-up sitting near you. Ready? Here are the steps. 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time counting. That is fine — it is only there to help you go quickly. Take one breath and get comfy. I expect you to feel calm, not worried. Fast is good, but right is better. 2. Read question one carefully. It might ask something like "Which part of your body do you use to see?" Say the answer out loud first, then type it in the box. I expect a short, clear answer, like "eyes" or "the eyes". 3. Now press Check and continue. The page will tell you if you got it right. If it says yes, smile — that is one for you! If it says no, read the correct answer and say it out loud once. Saying it helps your brain remember it. 4. Keep going, one question at a time. Read, answer, then press Check and continue. Do not skip ahead. I expect you to try every question, even the tricky ones. If you truly do not know, make your best guess and move on. 5. Remember your helpers as you go. Eyes see. Ears hear. Nose smells. Tongue tastes. Skin and hands feel. Head, arms, legs, hands and feet are body parts. If a question asks about staying healthy, think of washing hands, good food, clean water, sleep and play. 6. When you finish all twelve, look at your score. You need most of them right to pass this page. I expect you to be honest with yourself about which ones felt hard. 7. If you did not get enough right, do not worry. Press Run the sprint again and try once more. Mistakes are how we learn. The second try is usually much faster, because your brain now knows the words. 8. You will know the page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers. The page will show you that you have passed. That is your sign to stop and be proud. When you are done, come back and tell me your score and which question was the hardest. Take your time — there's no rush. Off you go, press Check and continue on question one! 🌟

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing the page called Solve Real Problems. Here is what this page is. There are six little stories about real life — at home, at the market, at school and outside. Each story asks you one question about your body, your senses, or staying clean and healthy. We do this so you can use what you learned in Unit 3 in real life, not just in a book. By the end, you will be able to say which sense you used and why, all by yourself. What you need: your eyes to read, your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. What I expect from you: read slowly, think first, then type your own answer in your own words. A good answer names the body part or sense, and says a little bit of why. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are the steps. 1. Read problem number one carefully. Read it twice. Ask yourself: what is this story really asking me? Point at the question word with your finger. I expect you to know what the question wants before you type anything. 2. Now think of your answer, then type it in the box and press Check answer. Type a short full sentence, like "I used my nose to smell it." If your brain goes empty, press Hint first and read the clue, then try again. I expect you to try your own answer before you press Hint. 3. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Give yourself a little smile! If it says not quite, read the question again and try one more time. Mistakes are how we learn. 4. Do the same thing for problems two, three, four, five and six. Read, think, type, press Check answer. One at a time, no rushing. The top part of the page is finished when all six say you are right. 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. This is your chance to say the answers again, and saying them again helps your brain remember them. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your answer, press Check answer, and press Hint only if you are stuck. I expect the same good work here — full sentences, your own words. 7. To move on, press the arrow on the right side of the slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you how far you have come and how many are left. 8. Keep going until the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the whole page is finished when all six problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Start with step one, read problem number one, and tell me what you think it is asking you. I am right here.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. Here is what it is. The page asks you a question about your body or your senses. You do not just say one word. You say your thinking out loud in writing: what you know, and why your answer makes sense. We do this because scientists always tell us WHY. By the end, you will be able to explain your ideas using our unit words like head, arms, legs, hands, eyes, ears, nose, mouth and senses. What I expect from you: try first, write in your own words, and use at least one of the key ideas shown under the prompt. Short is fine. One or two sentences is a great answer for Grade 1. You will need your reading eyes and, if writing is tricky, a grown-up sitting near you to help you type. Here is a small example of good thinking, so you can hear how it sounds. If I asked, "You hear a bird singing. Which sense told you?" I would write: "Hearing. I know we hear with our ears, and the sound came into my ears, so it is hearing." See? Answer, then the reason. There are 4 things to do on this page. 1. Read the prompt at the top, then read the key ideas under it. The prompt is the question. The key ideas are the words I want you to use. Read the prompt two times, slowly. Say it out loud if you can. I expect you to point at the key idea words and say them before you start writing. 2. Now write your explanation in the box. Put three little parts in it: what you know, the rule you used, and why your answer makes sense. When you are happy, press Check scientific ideas. If the page says it wants more, do not worry. Add one more sentence, maybe your reason or a key idea word, and press Check scientific ideas again. Mistakes are how we learn. 3. Next, press Show model explanation. This shows a good answer so you can compare. Read it and ask yourself: did I say the same idea? Did I use the key words? You do not have to copy it word for word. If yours is missing the reason, add it to your box. Then move on to the next prompt and do steps 1, 2 and 3 again. There are 4 prompts in total, so you will do this four times. 4. Last, look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Then use the same buttons you already know: type your answer, press Check scientific ideas, then Show model explanation. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide tell you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? When all 4 prompts have your own explanation in the box, each one uses the key ideas, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Only you can press those buttons, so your work is saved by you, not by me. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have read the first prompt, and tell me what it is asking. Then we will do it together.

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to the Games page! This is our fun practice time for Unit 3, Ourselves. The games ask you quick questions about your body and your five senses. Playing them helps the answers stick in your head, so you remember them fast. You only need your eyes, your fingers, and your thinking brain. Here are the three steps. 1. Find a game on the page and press Start game. A question will pop up with some answers to choose from. Read the question slowly, then pick the answer you think is right. You get a star for every round you get right! I expect you to think first, not just tap fast. If you are not sure, whisper the question to yourself again, or touch the body part on YOU. Your ears, your nose, your eyes — they are right there to help you. 2. When the game ends, press Play again. Playing again gives you more chances to win more stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars — that means you did it really well! I expect you to keep trying, even if you miss one. Mistakes are how we learn. If you got one wrong, read the little explanation, say the right answer out loud, then play again. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Start game, answer the rounds, then Play again until that game has all its stars. Then move to the next one. I expect you to finish one game fully before you start a new one. That way your brain learns one thing at a time. You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars — the page finishes by itself when they are all mastered. No button to press at the end, just full stars everywhere! Ready? Press Start game on the first game, then come and tell me how it went. Take your time — there's no rush.

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Science Words page in Unit 3, Ourselves. This page has ten body words: head, arms, legs, hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, mouth and senses. We learn them so you can name your own body parts and say what each one does. By the end, you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You will need your voice, your body to point with, and your fingers for typing. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. Then point to that part on your own body. I expect you to say the word out loud after the Listen voice, not just read it quietly. Step 2. Now say the word out loud again, and say the meaning in your own words. Not the same words as the page — your words. For example, for "hands" you might say, "the parts I hold my cup with." A good answer names the part and says what it does. Step 3. Now type one sentence using that word. Then press Check sentence. A good sentence starts with a capital letter, ends with a full stop, and uses the word properly, like "I wash my hands before I eat." Read what the checker says to you, and if it asks for a fix, try again. Then do steps 1, 2 and 3 for every word on the page, one word at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 4. When every word is done, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the science words. Only press it after all ten words, because it tells your teacher you finished them. Step 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same things you did before: listen, say the word, say the meaning, and use the buttons on the slide. Step 6. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Keep going, one slide at a time. Step 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That closes the deck nicely. You will know the page is finished when the I explored the science words button is pressed and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Do step 1 with your first word, then tell me your sentence — I'll be right here. 🙂

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! I am Wehel Tutor, and today I am your teacher for Unit 4: Materials in my World. This page is the Unit Overview. It is like looking at a map before a trip. It shows what we will learn and what you will be able to do at the end. In this unit you will learn about materials. A material is what a thing is made from, like wood, metal, plastic or cloth. You will learn feeling words too, like hard, soft, rough and smooth. What I expect from you: look at the page carefully, listen well, and say your ideas out loud. There are no wrong answers on this page. You just need your eyes, your ears and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1. Read the Unit Overview on your screen. Look at the part that says what this unit is about and what you will be able to do. If you see a little speaker, press Listen and listen all the way to the end. Do it well by keeping your eyes on the words while the voice reads. I expect you to read or listen to the whole thing, not just the first line. Step 2. Now say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud to your grown-up, or type it to me. You can start like this: "I think I will learn about..." A good answer has one or two ideas in it, for example materials, or how things feel. I expect one full sentence from you, in your own words. Do not copy the screen. Step 3. When you have said your idea, press Continue. That button takes you to The Lesson, where the real learning starts. Do it well by only pressing Continue after Step 1 and Step 2 are truly done. I expect you to press it yourself, so the page knows you finished. You will know the page is finished when you have listened or read, said your own sentence, and pressed Continue and landed on The Lesson. Take your time — there's no rush. Come back and tell me your sentence from Step 2, and I will listen! 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for The Lesson page in Unit 4, Materials in my World. This page teaches you four big ideas. You will learn what a material is, how materials feel, why we pick the right material for a job, and how to sort things into groups. By the end you can pick up any object at home and say what it is made from and how it feels. You need your eyes, your ears, your hands and your voice. A pencil is nice too. Let's start! 1. Find the first concept at the top of the page. Read it slowly, word by word. Then press Listen and hear it read to you while you follow along. I expect you to read AND listen to each one, not rush. There are four concepts, so do this four times. 2. Each concept has an example at the end. Say the example out loud, in a big clear voice. Then do it for real with things near you. For concept one, pick up three things and say what material each one is made from, like "This spoon is metal." For concept two, find one hard thing and one soft thing, then one rough thing and one smooth thing, and say the word as you touch it. I expect real objects from your home, not just reading. 3. For concept three, look at a cooking pot and a window. Say what each is made from and why that material is good for that job. For concept four, collect six objects and put them in two groups by material, like wood in one group and plastic in the other. Then mix them up and sort the same six again, but this time by how they feel, hard in one group and soft in the other. I expect you to say your sorting rule out loud, like "These are all metal."

4. When you have read all four concepts and tried all the examples, go to the bottom of the page and press I studied the concepts. Only press it when you really did all four. That is your promise to yourself that you did the work. 5. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same four concepts, one idea on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Read it, listen if there is a Listen button, and say the idea back in your own words before you move on. 6. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide, they show you which slide you are on. Use the same buttons on every slide, one slide at a time. Take your time, there is no rush. 7. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have been through all the slides. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you have done the whole lesson! Ready? Start with step one, then come back and tell me what material your three objects were made from. I will be right here. 😊

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Hello! Today we are learning our Science Words for Unit 4. This page has six special words: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. These words help you tell people how a thing feels. By the end, you will be able to say each word, say what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, your ears, and your fingers for touching things near you. Let's start with something small. 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. I expect you to listen right to the end, not rush past it. 2. Now say the word out loud, in your big voice. Then say the meaning in your OWN words — not the same words on the page. For example, for "hard" you might say, "it does not squash when I press it." Saying it your way shows me you really understand. 3. Next, think of one real thing near you that matches the word. Touch it if you can. A stone for hard. A pillow for soft. This makes the word stick in your head. 4. Now type your own sentence with the word in it, then press Check sentence. A good sentence names a real thing and uses the word, like "My table is hard." Read what the checker tells you. If it asks you to try again, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. 5. Do the same four things for every word on the page: read it, press Listen, say it and its meaning, then type a sentence and press Check sentence. Take your time — there's no rush. Six words, one at a time. 6. When you have finished every word, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the science words. Only press it when all six are done, because that button tells your teacher you did the whole page. 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you used before: press Listen, say the word out loud, say the meaning your way, and type your sentence and press Check sentence. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you how far you have come. 9. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. That closes the deck. You will know the page is finished when the I explored the science words button is pressed and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you have done it all! Ready? Start with word number one, and tell me when you have pressed Listen. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's look at this page together. This page is called Explore the Concept. On it you will meet four little discoveries about materials. A material is what a thing is made from, like wood, metal, plastic or cloth. We do this page so you can look, think and say your own idea — just like a real scientist. By the end you will be able to name materials and describe them with words like hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. What you need: your eyes, your fingers, and your thinking. You can have a grown-up nearby to help you type. What I expect from you: try your own idea first, in your own words. A short sentence is perfect. Guessing is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Step 1. At the top of the page you will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3 and 4. Press tab 1. Read the little story there and look carefully at the picture or model. Take your time. I expect you to notice one thing, like what the object is made from, or how it would feel in your hand. Step 2. Under the picture there is a discovery question. Read it slowly, twice. Think first, before you type. Ask yourself: what is it made from, and how does it feel? Step 3. Type your idea in the box. Use your own words and try to use one science word, like hard, soft, bendy or smooth. Then press Check my idea. I expect a real try, not an empty box. Step 4. Now read what the page says back to you. If it says Exactly!, brilliant work — the tab gets a tick. If it says Look again, that is okay. Press Hint, read the clue, and try once more with a new idea. Step 5. Press tab 2 and do the very same thing: read, look, think, type, press Check my idea. Then do tab 3, then tab 4. One tab at a time, please. Do not rush ahead. Step 6. Look at your four tabs. The page is finished when every discovery question has a tick. If one tab has no tick, go back to it and try again with the Hint. Step 7. Now scroll down to the slides under the page. These are the same discoveries again, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons you already know: read, type your idea, press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 9. Keep going until you reach the last slide. There, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. How will you know the page is finished? All four tabs have a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then it is complete. When you get to the end, come back and tell me one thing you found out. Take your time — there's no rush. Ready? Press tab 1 now.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes that show our science ideas. We use them because materials are easier to understand when you can SEE them and turn them around. By the end, you will be able to name materials and say how they feel. All you need is your eyes, your finger on the screen, and your talking voice. There are 3 steps. Here they are. Step 1: Look at the first model, "What Is It Made From?". It shows what objects are made from, like wood, metal, plastic and glass. If the picture moves, drag it slowly with your finger to turn it all the way around. Press any buttons on it to see what changes. I expect you to say out loud one material you can see. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Look at the second model, "How Does It Feel?". This one is about our property words: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. Drag it to turn it, and press its buttons to see each property. I expect you to say two of these words out loud as you look. Good looking means slow looking! Step 3: Look at the third model, "The Right Material for the Job". It shows why we pick a material for each job, like glass for a window. Turn it with your finger and press its buttons. I expect you to point at one thing and tell me why that material is right for it. Step 4: Look at the fourth model, "Sorting Materials". Sorting means putting things into groups that are the same in some way. Drag it and press its buttons to see the groups. I expect you to name one group you see, like "all the wooden things". Step 5: Now read the caption under each model. The caption is the little sentence below the picture. Press Listen under each one and listen carefully to the words. I expect you to listen to all four, not just one. Step 6: When you have looked at all four models and heard all four captions, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Press it only when you really have seen them all. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models and the page shows it is done. Then come back and tell me your favourite model — I would love to hear!

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are working on the Worked Examples page for Unit 4, Materials in my World. A worked example is a question with the answer already worked out for you. We do this so you can see how a good scientist thinks, step by step. By the end, you will be better at saying what things are made from, and why. You need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a pencil and paper. Let's go! 1. Look at the first worked example on the page. Read the question slowly, all by yourself. Try to answer it in your head first, before you look at any solution. I expect you to have a go, even if you are not sure. A guess is fine — guessing is how scientists start! 2. Now press Show worked solution on that example. Read the solution line by line. Ask yourself: did I say the same thing? If yes, well done! If not, that is okay — mistakes are how we learn. I expect you to notice one thing the solution did that you did not. 3. Do the same for every worked example. There are 8 of them. Read the question, think of your answer, then press Show worked solution and compare. Take your time — there is no rush. I expect you to open all 8, not just the easy ones. 4. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It tells you how many examples you have opened. Keep going until the counter shows all 8 are open. That means the top part of the page is complete. 5. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 6. On each slide, use the same buttons as before. Read the question, think of your answer, then show the solution and compare. I expect you to say your answer out loud each time — even a quiet whisper counts! 7. When you finish a slide, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are in the deck. 8. Keep going until you reach the last slide. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows every example is open, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready to start? Read the first question, then tell me what you think the answer is. I would love to hear your thinking! 🌟

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice in Unit 4, Materials in my World. Guided Practice is where you try questions all by yourself, with me close by to help. We do it because the best way to learn is to have a go. By the end, you will be able to say what things are made from, describe how they feel with words like hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff, and say why a material is right for a job. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. You can also pick up real things around you and feel them. That is real science! Here is what I expect from you: try first, then ask for help. Answer in a few words, like "Metal" or "Soft, so it is comfy." Do not worry about a wrong answer. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Look at the page. There are 12 practice questions. Read one question, slowly, all the way to the end. Then read it again. Work the answer out on paper or in your head. If the question is about a real thing, like a stone or a pillow, go and touch one. Ask yourself two questions: what is it made from, and how does it feel? I expect you to think before you type, even if it takes a minute. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2: Type your answer in the box and press Check my answer. Write in your own words, not just one letter. If you are stuck, press Give me a hint. You can press it up to three times, and each hint tells you a little bit more. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working. I expect you to try your own answer first, before the hints. That is how your brain grows strong. Step 3: Do the same thing for every question, one at a time, until each one is right. If an answer is not right, do not skip it. Read the hint, think again, and try once more. Then move to the next question. I expect you to finish all 12, not just the easy ones. Step 4: Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it and press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need them. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. When you reach the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All 12 questions are answered and right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is your work saved. I do not press it for you — you do, because it is your work. Ready? Go and read question one now, then tell me your answer and I will check it with you. 🙂

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Learn the Method" page. A method is a way to work something out, step by step. On this page there are 4 methods about materials. You will read one step, then the next, then the next — like climbing little stairs. By the end you will know how to test a material and say what it is like: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy or stiff. What you need: your eyes, your reading voice, and maybe a pencil. What I expect from you: read every step out loud, do not rush, and think about one real thing at home that matches the step. Take your time — there's no rush. Here are all the steps. Do them in order. 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read the first step out loud, slowly. Then press the button that says Show me the next step. I expect you to read before you press — the button is not a race! 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step. Say each new step out loud as it appears. Keep going until the page says Method complete. When you see those words, that method is done. Good job! 3. Now do the very same thing for the other methods. There are 4 methods in all. For each one: read the first step out loud, press Show me the next step again and again, and stop when it says Method complete. I expect all 4 methods to reach Method complete. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same methods on it. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons to move through the steps, saying each one out loud. 5. When a slide is finished, press the arrow on the right side. That takes you to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on. I expect you to do every slide, not just the first one. 6. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. How will you know the page is finished? Easy! Every method says Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is when you are done. Off you go with step 1. Come back and tell me when your first method says Method complete, and I will check it with you. 🌟

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are playing the Games on our Materials page. 🎮

These games ask you about materials. Materials are what things are made from, like wood, metal, cloth and glass. The games also use our feeling words: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. We play them so these words stay in your head, like a song you remember. You need your eyes, your fingers to tap, and your thinking brain. You can also touch things near you to help you feel the answer. Here is what I expect from you: read each question slowly, think before you tap, and try your very best. Wrong answers are fine. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 3 steps. Here they are. 1. Find a game card on the page and press Start game. A question will come up with some choices. Read it twice. Then tap the one answer you think is right. You get a star for every round you get right. Do this for all four rounds of that game. I expect you to think first, then tap, not tap fast. 2. When the game ends, press Play again. This lets you win more stars. Keep playing that game until it has all its stars. A game with all its stars is mastered. That means you really know it. If a question is tricky, say the word out loud and think of something at home that feels like that. I expect you to keep trying, even after a wrong answer. 3. Now do the same with every other game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, press Play again, and fill up the stars. Take your time. There is no rush at all. You will know the page is finished when every game has all its stars. The page then finishes by itself. You do not have to press anything special. 🌟

Ready? Press Start game on the first game, then tell me how it went!

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Quick Reference. Quick Reference is like a little map of Unit 4. It holds our big ideas and our science words on one page: material, hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. We read it so the words stay in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what a material is and use these words to talk about things in your home. You need your eyes, your voice, and one finger to press the buttons. There are three steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Read the Quick Reference slowly. Look at the top of the page and read one line at a time. When you see a speaker button, press Listen and hear the word said out loud. Then say the word back with your own voice. I expect you to touch something near you while you read. Read "hard", then press a stone or a table. Read "soft", then press a pillow. This makes the words stick. Step 2: Say the key facts in your own words. Close your eyes for a moment, then say them out loud, like you are teaching a friend. You can say it like this: "A material is what a thing is made from. Wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper and cloth are materials. Hard does not press in. Soft presses in. Rough is bumpy. Smooth has no bumps. Bendy can bend. Stiff will not bend." I do not want you to copy the page word for word. Your own words are better. If you forget one, peek at the page, then say it again without looking. Step 3: Press Reference reviewed at the bottom. Scroll down to the end of the page and find that button. Only press it when you have really read every line and said the facts out loud. Pressing it saves your work, so it must come from you. You will know the page is finished when you have read the whole Quick Reference, said the key facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed at the bottom. Now start with Step 1. Tell me when you have read it, and I will listen to your own words. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Experiments page for Unit 4, Materials in my World. On this page you become a real scientist. You will touch things, bend things and sort things. You will find out what each thing is made from. That is called its material. You will also use our feeling words: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. Why do we do this? Because science is not just reading. Scientists find out by trying. By the end you will be able to name materials and say how they feel. What you need: a pencil, a few safe things from your home, and a grown-up nearby. Never use hot, sharp or breakable things. Ask your grown-up first if you need water. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first experiment on the page. Read the title and the words. Then press Listen and hear it read to you. I expect you to listen right to the end, then say out loud what things you must collect. Now go and get those things and put them on the table in front of you. Step 2. Before you touch anything, make a prediction. A prediction is what you think will happen. Say it out loud, like this: "I think the spoon will be hard." I expect one guess before you start. Guessing wrong is fine. Scientists guess first every single time. Step 3. Now do the experiment. Touch, press or bend each thing slowly. Look carefully. Then write your answer in the box. Write what you noticed and use one of our words: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy or stiff. A good answer names the thing and the word, like "the cloth is soft and bendy". Even a few words is great work. Step 4. When you have done that experiment and filled the box, press Mark complete under it. Only press it when you really did it. That button tells your teacher, "I finished this one."

Step 5. Now do the same for the other experiments. There are 6 in all. For each one: press Listen, get the things, make a prediction, do it, write in the box, then press Mark complete. Take your time. There is no rush. Step 6. When all 6 say complete, go to the bottom of the page and press Finish activities. Well done, that is the top part of the page done. Step 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. It has the same experiments, one experiment on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Step 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, then do it, then write your answer, then Mark complete. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 9. Keep going until the last slide. On that last slide, press Finish activities. How will you know the page is finished? Every experiment shows Mark complete, you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom of the page, and you have pressed Finish activities on the last slide too. Then you are done! Ready? Start with Step 1 and tell me what your first experiment asks you to collect.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Solve Real Problems" page. On this page you use what you know about materials in real life. A real problem is like a question from a real day, such as "why is a raincoat made from plastic?" We do this because knowing your materials helps you choose the right thing for the right job. You will need your eyes, your thinking brain, and maybe a pencil to jot ideas. Let's look at that together, step by step. Here is what I expect from you today: read slowly, think first, and use our science words like hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. Answers must come from your own head, not from me. There are 4 steps. Step 1. Read the first problem carefully. There are 6 problems on this page. Read it twice, and ask yourself, "What is this question really asking me?" Point at the object it talks about and say what material it is made from. I expect you to know the object and the material before you write anything. Step 2. Now work it out and type it in the box. Write your answer in one or two little sentences. A good answer says the material AND why, like this: "It is made from wood, because wood is stiff and strong." Then press Check answer. If your brain feels stuck, press Hint first and think again. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 3. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done! Then go to the next problem and do the same thing: read, think, type, press Check answer. Do this for all 6 problems, one at a time. I expect you to try each one yourself before you press Hint. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same problems, one problem on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it with the same buttons you already know: type your answer, press Check answer, press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All 6 problems will say your answer is right, and you will have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are done! Ready? Tell me the first problem you see, and what you think it is asking. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today we are on the "Explain Your Thinking" page. Here you do not just say an answer — you say WHY. That is what scientists do. We are doing this so you can use our unit words: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. You will need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby to help you type. Here are the steps. Step 1. Look at the first prompt on the page. There are 4 prompts in all. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it to you. Under the prompt you will see some key ideas — these are the words I want to hear in your answer. I expect you to read the prompt twice before you write. Step 2. Now write your answer in the box. A good answer has two parts: what you think, and why. Like this: "It is made from cloth, because cloth is soft and bendy." Then press Check scientific ideas. If the page asks for more, add one more sentence with a key word in it, and press Check scientific ideas again. Step 3. Now press Show model explanation. This shows you a good answer so you can compare. Do not worry if yours uses different words — look for the key ideas. If yours is missing one, that is fine; just notice it and use it next time. Then do the same three steps for prompts 2, 3 and 4. Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. They have the same prompts, one prompt on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same as before: write your answer, press Check scientific ideas, then press Show model explanation. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Step 5. Keep going slide by slide until the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when all 4 explanations use the key ideas and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you have read the first prompt, and I will help you with it. 🙂

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Science Fluency page. Let me tell you what it is. Science Fluency is a quick sprint. A sprint means going fast! There are 12 short questions about materials. They ask things like what a spoon is made from, and if a stone is hard or soft. We do this so the words come to your mind quickly, without you having to stop and think for a long time. By the end, you will say "wood", "metal", "hard", "soft", "bendy" and "stiff" nice and fast. What you need: your eyes, your brain, and your fingers for typing. A grown-up can sit with you and help you type. What I expect from you: try your best on every question, answer with short words, and keep going even if one feels tricky. A quick "not sure" answer is better than stopping. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see your time. It counts while you work. Do not worry about it! It is just to show you how fast you went. Take a deep breath and get ready. Step 2. Read the first question slowly, then answer fast. Type your answer in the box. Short is fine. If it asks what a sufuria is made from, you can just type the material word. Then press Check & continue. Step 3. Keep going, one question at a time. There are 12 in the sprint. After each answer, press Check & continue to move on. Do not skip any. Answer all 12, even the ones you are unsure about. Step 4. Use your touching words when the question asks how something feels. Your six words are hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. Picture the thing in your head and pretend you are touching it. Step 5. For "why" questions, give a short reason. For example, if it asks why we use glass for a window, say what glass lets you do. One little reason is enough. I expect a reason, not just yes or no. Step 6. When you finish all 12, the page will show you how you did. You need most of them right to pass. Look at any you got wrong and read what the right answer was. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 7. If you did not get enough right, press Run the sprint again. Do not feel sad about this. The second try is nearly always better, because now you have practised. Step 8. Keep going until one sprint has enough right. When that happens, the page counts as finished. That is how you will know you are done: the page tells you your sprint was good enough, and it does not ask you to run it again. Now, off you go. Press your first question and start the sprint. Tell me when you finish, and tell me your time — I would love to hear it! 🌟

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called The Lesson. On this page you will learn about pushes and pulls. A push moves a thing away from you. A pull brings a thing near you. By the end you will be able to say push or pull for things all around your home. You need your eyes, your voice, a clear space on the floor, and one small toy or ball. A grown-up can help you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, say the words out loud, and really try each little action with your hands. There are four things to do on this page. 1. Read the five concepts, one at a time. At the top of the page you will see the first concept. Read it slowly. Then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listening while you read helps the words stick. I expect you to finish one concept before you start the next one. 2. Do the example out loud and with your hands. Under each concept there is an example, like "push a door shut and say push". Say the word push or pull out loud while you do it. Then try it with your own things at home, like a toy car, a spoon or a cushion. A good job looks like this: you moved something, and you said push or pull for it. 3. Read every concept, then press "I studied the concepts". Do not press it early. Press it only when you have read all five and tried all five examples. That button tells the page you have done your reading. 4. Go through the slides at the bottom. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same concepts. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on each slide. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. 5. Finish the last slide. Keep going, one slide at a time, until the dots show you are at the end. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to look at every slide, not skip ahead. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed "I studied the concepts" and pressed the finish button on the last slide. Now let's start with step one. Read the first concept, Many Ways to Move, and press Listen. Tell me when you are done, and tell me one way your body can move. 😊

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Science Words page. This page has the ten special words of Unit 5. They are Push, Pull, Force, Move, Stop, Fast, Slow, Turn, Roll and Slide. We learn these words so you can say what is happening when things move. By the end you will be able to hear each word, say what it means in your own words, and use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, your ears, and your fingers to type. Here are all the steps. Step 1. Look at the first word card on the page. Read the word, then read the little line that tells you what it means. Do this slowly, with your finger under the word if that helps. I expect you to read the word and its meaning before you press anything. Step 2. Press Listen on that word. Listen carefully to how the word sounds. Then say it out loud, just like the voice said it. Say it once more if it felt hard. I expect to hear your voice, not a whisper in your head. Step 3. Now say the meaning in your OWN words. Do not copy the line on the screen. For Push you could say, "I move it away from me." For Pull you could say, "I bring it to me." A good answer is short and true, and it sounds like you. Step 4. Now type a sentence with that word in the sentence box, then press Check sentence. Make your sentence about your real life, like "I push the door shut" or "I pull my sock on." A good sentence has the word in it, starts with a big letter, and ends with a full stop. Try your best spelling; you are Grade 1, so a small mistake is fine. Step 5. Read what the checker says back to you. It may say well done, or it may give you a tip. If it gives a tip, fix your sentence and press Check sentence again. I expect you to read the message, not skip it. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 6. Do steps 1 to 5 again for every word on the page: Push, Pull, Force, Move, Stop, Fast, Slow, Turn, Roll and Slide. Take your time — there's no rush. Ten words is a lot, so you may stop for a drink of water and come back. Step 7. When every word has been read, heard, said and used in a sentence, press the button that says I explored the science words at the bottom. Only press it when all ten are really done. That button tells the page you finished this part. Step 8. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same words, one word on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. This part is your practice, so the words stay in your head. Step 9. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen to the word, say it out loud, say what it means in your own words, then type a sentence and press Check sentence. When that slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, like footprints. Step 10. Keep going, slide by slide, until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to do every slide, not jump to the end. You will know the page is finished when two things are true: the button I explored the science words has been pressed, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then you are all done for this page. Now start with Step 1, and tell me when you have pressed Listen on your first word. I am right here with you.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 5: Pushes and Pulls. This page is our first look at the unit. It tells you what we will learn and what you will be able to do at the end. We are doing it so your brain knows what is coming, like looking at a map before a walk. By the end of this unit, you will be able to spot a push and a pull all around your home. You need only your eyes, your voice, and your two hands. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, listen carefully, and talk out loud. There are three steps. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the page about pushes and pulls. Where you see a speaker picture, press Listen and hear the words too. Read with your eyes and listen with your ears at the same time. I expect you to go slowly and not rush. Step 2: Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Say it out loud, even if a grown-up is not there. A good answer sounds like this: "I will learn about pushes and pulls, and how they make things move." Use the words push and pull in your sentence. I expect one or two sentences, in your own voice, not copied word for word. Step 3: Press Continue to go to The Lesson. This button takes you to the next part. Only press it after you have read the page and said your sentence. I expect you to be ready and excited for the lesson! You will know this page is finished when you have read it, listened to it, said your own sentence, and pressed Continue. Ready? Start with step one, and tell me when you have read it. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Explore the Concept page. On this page you will play like a scientist. You will push things and pull things, and you will say what you see. A push moves a thing away from you. A pull brings a thing near you. Both of them are called a force. By the end you will be able to spot a push and a pull all around you. What you need: your eyes, your hands, and something small to try with, like a ball, a toy car or a shoe. A grown-up can sit near you to help. What I expect from you: guess first, then look, then tell me in your own words. Use the words push, pull, force, fast, slow, roll and slide. Short answers are fine. Wrong guesses are fine too — mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1. Look at the top of the page. You will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3, 4. Press tab 1. Read the little story there and look at the picture or model. Take your time and really look. I expect you to notice one thing before you answer, like "the ball went far" or "the box did not roll". Step 2. Under the picture there is a discovery question. Read it, then think for a moment. What do you think happens first? Type your idea in the box in your own words, then press Check my idea. If the page says Look again, do not worry. Press Hint, read it, and try once more. When it says Exactly!, the tab gets a little tick. That tick means you got it! Step 3. Now do the same for tab 2, tab 3 and tab 4. Press the tab, read, think, type, press Check my idea. Keep going until every tab has a tick. The page is done when all four discovery questions are answered right. I expect you to try each one yourself first, before you press Hint. Step 4. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom of the page. It is a deck of slides with the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons as before: type your idea, press Check my idea, press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How you will know you are finished: every numbered tab has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Remember, I do not tick it for you — you press the buttons, because it is your work. Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you see. Take your time — there's no rush.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes that show our unit ideas. There are 5 of them, all about pushes and pulls. By the end, you will be able to look at each model and say push or pull out loud. You need your eyes, your finger for the buttons, and your talking voice. Let's start! 1. Look at the first model, Many Ways to Move. Move your finger or mouse over it and drag it to turn it around. If it has buttons, press them and watch what changes. I expect you to look for a few seconds and tell me one thing you see moving. 2. Now the second model, Push Moves Away, Pull Brings Near. Drag it to turn it. Watch which way the thing goes. I expect you to say push if it goes away from you, and pull if it comes near you. 3. Next is the third model, Move, Stop, and Turn. Press its buttons one at a time, not all at once. Watch it go, watch it stop, watch it turn. I expect you to name all three: move, stop, turn. 4. Now the fourth model, Fast and Slow, Roll and Slide. Drag it and press its buttons. Look for the fast one and the slow one. I expect you to tell me which push was bigger, the fast one or the slow one. 5. The fifth model is Pushes and Pulls Around Us. Turn it and look at the things in it, like doors, swings and carts. I expect you to point at one thing and say push or pull for it. 6. Under every model there is a caption. That is the little sentence that tells you what the picture shows. Read it slowly, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. 7. Now press the Listen button under each caption. Listen carefully to the words. Try saying one word back, like push, pull or force. Do this for all 5 models. 8. Last step! When you have looked at all 5 models and listened to all 5 captions, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models. That button keeps the record of your work, so only press it at the end. Ready? Start with model one and tell me what you see.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Learn the Method" page. This page shows you methods. A method is a way to do something, step by step, like a recipe. Our methods are all about pushes and pulls. By the end you will know how to try a push or pull the right way, and how to say what you saw. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. Let's start with something small. What I expect from you: read each step, say it out loud, and think about it for a moment before you press the next button. Slow and careful beats fast. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step. Now say that step out loud in your own voice. When you have said it, press the button that says Show me the next step. I expect you to read and speak, not just press. Step 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step. Say each new step out loud too. Keep going until the page says Method complete. That tells you this method is finished. Step 3. Now do the same for every method. There are 4 methods on this page. For each one, read a step, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, and keep going until it says Method complete. All 4 must reach the end. Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same methods. Press Start on the first slide. Then use the same buttons on that slide, just like before. Step 5. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right. That takes you to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Watch the dots move along. Step 6. Do every slide this way. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know the page is finished? All 4 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. One more thing from me: as you go, try one push and one pull at home with a toy. That makes the words stick. Ready? Go and do Step 1, then come back and tell me what your first method was about. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello, my learner! Today we are on the Worked Examples page for Unit 5, Pushes and Pulls. A worked example is a question with the answer already shown, step by step. We look at them so you can see how a good answer is built. By the end, you will know how to say if something is a push or a pull, and what a force does. All you need is your thinking brain, and a pencil and paper if you like. Here are the steps. There are 5. 1. Look at the first worked example on your screen. Read the question slowly, all by yourself or with your grown-up. Before you press anything, say your own answer out loud, like "push!" or "pull!". I expect you to try first — a try is never wrong, it is brave. 2. Now press Show worked solution on that same example. Read the answer line by line and compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I say the same thing? If yes, smile big. If not, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. 3. Do the same for all 8 worked examples. Read, guess, then press Show worked solution and check. Look at the counter at the top of the page — it counts how many you have opened. I expect you to open every single one, so the counter shows all 8. 4. Now go under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: read, think, then show the answer. Press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide tell you where you are. 5. Keep going slide by slide until you reach the last one. On the last slide, press the finish button. I expect you to say each answer out loud before you look — that is how it sticks in your head. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 8 opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Off you go with step 1. Tell me the question you see, and what you think the answer is. Take your time — there's no rush.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today we are doing Guided Practice for Unit 5, Pushes and Pulls. This page has 12 short questions about pushes and pulls. We do it so the two big words stay in your head: a push moves a thing away from you, and a pull brings a thing toward you. Both of them are called a force. By the end you will be able to look at any door, ball or drawer and say push or pull. You will need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here is the whole plan, step by step. 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Then think about the answer in your head, or draw it on your paper. I expect you to try first, even if you feel unsure. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Write a short, clear answer, like "a pull" or "faster". If you can, add why, like "a pull, because it comes to me." That is a really strong answer. 3. If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. Read one hint, then think again before you ask for the next one. That is how good scientists work. 4. If you are still stuck after the hints, press Show next step. It gives you one line of the working. Read it, then finish the rest yourself. I expect the last bit to come from you. 5. If your answer is not right, do not worry at all. Mistakes are how we learn. Read the question again, look at what went wrong, and type a new answer. Then press Check my answer again. 6. Do this for every question, one at a time, until all 12 are right. Do not skip any. When each question is right, this part of the page is done. 7. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide to begin. 8. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: type your answer and press Check my answer, and use Give me a hint or Show next step if you need help. Try to use fewer hints this time, because you have already practised. 9. To go to the next slide, press the arrow on the right. Look at the little dots under the slide. They show you where you are and how many are left. 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you have done them all. You will know the page is finished when all 12 questions show as right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Read question one and tell me your answer — I am right here with you.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today we are on the Quick Reference page. This page is like a little pocket card. It holds the big words and big ideas of Unit 5, Pushes and Pulls, all in one place. We read it so the words stay in your head. By the end, you will be able to say what a push, a pull and a force are, all by yourself. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here are the steps. 1. Read the Quick Reference. Look at the words on the page and read them slowly, one at a time. The big ones are Push, Pull, Force, Roll and Slide. Where you see a speaker button, press Listen and listen to the word. I expect you to read every word once, not rush. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Do the words with your body. As you read Push, push your hands away from you. As you read Pull, bring your hands back to you. Do this for Roll and Slide too. I expect your hands to move, not just your eyes. This helps your brain remember. 3. Say the key facts in your own words. Now close your eyes for a moment and say them out loud, like you are teaching a friend. Try these: a push moves a thing away from me, a pull brings a thing to me, and both are called a force. I expect your own words, not perfect words. If you get stuck, peek at the page, then say it again without looking. 4. Give one real example for each word. Say one thing you push at home, and one thing you pull at home. A door, a drawer, a chair, a swing — all good. I expect two real things from your own house. That is how the words become yours. 5. Press Reference reviewed. This button is at the bottom of the page. Press it only after you have read the words and said them out loud. I expect you to press it yourself — that is how the page keeps your work. You will know the page is finished when you have said the key facts in your own words and the Reference reviewed button has been pressed. Now start with step 1, and tell me when you are done. 🙂

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text:
Hello, scientist! Today you are a real scientist. This page has six little experiments about pushes and pulls. A push moves a thing away from you. A pull brings a thing to you. Both are called a force. By the end, you will have felt forces with your own hands, and you will be able to say what you saw. Here is what I expect from you. Do each experiment for real, with your hands, not just in your head. Look carefully. Then write or draw what you noticed, using the words push, pull, force, fast, slow, roll and slide. You will need a small ball, a toy car, some string, and a clear space on the floor. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. Step 1. Look at the first experiment on the page. Read what it says, and press Listen to hear it read to you. Listening and reading together helps the words stick. Step 2. Go and get the things it names. Put them on the floor or table in front of you. A good scientist gets ready first. Step 3. Before you touch anything, make a prediction. A prediction is what you think will happen. Say it out loud, like this: "I think the ball will go fast." Predicting first is what real scientists do. Step 4. Now do the activity. Push or pull the thing slowly and watch it closely. Do it two or three times so you are sure. Notice what changed: did it move, stop, turn, go fast, go slow, roll or slide? Step 5. Write your answer in the box under the activity. One good sentence is plenty, and you can draw a small picture too. I would love to see a word like push, pull or force in your sentence. If writing is hard, say it out loud to your grown-up first, then write it. Step 6. Press Mark complete under that activity. Only press it when you have really done it with your hands. That button says, "Yes, I did this one."

Step 7. Now do the same for the next experiment, and the next, until all six are done. Read, press Listen, get the things, predict, do it, write in the box, then press Mark complete. Take your time. There is no rush. Step 8. When every activity has a tick, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. That tells the page you have finished all six. Step 9. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same experiments, one experiment on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 10. On each slide, use the same buttons as before: Listen, write in the box, then Mark complete. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, like steps on a path. Step 11. On the last slide, press Finish activities again. When all the activities are ticked and you have pressed Finish activities, the page is done. That is how you will know you are finished. Ready? Start with Step 1, and tell me when you have your things. Then tell me your prediction, and we will find out together!

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Unit 5 games about pushes and pulls. Games help your brain remember the words push, pull and force. When you play, you get stars for right answers. All you need is your finger to tap, your eyes to read, and your thinking brain. Let's start! There are 3 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Pick one game and press Start game. Read the question slowly, then read all four choices before you tap. Think: does this move a thing away from me, or bring it near me? Away is a push. Near is a pull. Tap your answer. If you get it right, you earn a star. If not, that's okay — read the little explanation, because mistakes are how we learn. I expect you to try every round, not skip any. Step 2: When the game ends, press Play again. This gives you more chances to earn stars. A game is mastered when it has all its stars. Say the answer out loud before you tap — that helps it stick in your memory. I expect you to keep playing that same game until its stars are full. Step 3: Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game, answer the rounds, press Play again until each one is mastered. Take your time — there's no rush. I expect you to finish one game before you jump to the next. How will you know you are done? When every game has all its stars, the page finishes by itself. No button to press at the end — the page does that part for you. Go ahead and press Start game on your first game. Tell me when you have played one round, and tell me one question you got. I'll be right here! 🌟

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Science Fluency. Fluency means quick and sure. You already know about pushes and pulls. Now we make those ideas fast in your head, like knowing your own name. There are 12 quick questions, and a timer at the top counts your time. You do not need to rush and worry — you just need to think and answer. What I expect from you: read each question once, say the answer in your head, then type it. Use our science words: push, pull, force, roll, slide, fast, slow, turn. Guessing wildly is not our way. Thinking, then answering, is our way. Get a pencil and paper near you too, in case you want to draw a little picture to help. Here are all the steps, one after the other. Step 1: Look at the top of the page and find the timer. Take one slow breath. Then start the sprint. I expect you to be calm and ready, not worried. Step 2: Read question one. Ask yourself the little question: does the thing go away from me, or come towards me? Away is a push. Towards is a pull. I expect you to picture it with your own hands. Step 3: Type your answer in the box. Short words are fine, like "push" or "pull" or "force". I expect a clear word, not a long story. Step 4: Press Check & continue. This shows if you were right and takes you to the next question. I expect you to press it yourself for every single question. Step 5: If the question is about how hard you push, remember your body. A soft push makes a thing go slow. A big push makes it go fast. I expect you to use the words fast and slow. Step 6: If the question is about shape, remember round things roll and flat things slide. A ball rolls. A shoe slides. I expect you to look at the shape in your mind first. Step 7: If the question asks how to stop something or turn it, remember this: it takes a force to start, a force to stop, and a force to turn. I expect you to use the word force here. Step 8: If you get one wrong, do not feel sad. Read what the page tells you, say it once out loud, and then press Check & continue to keep going. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 9: Keep going the same way until all 12 questions are done. Type, press Check & continue, type, press Check & continue. I expect you to finish all twelve, not stop in the middle. Step 10: At the end, look at your score. You need most of them right. That means nearly all of them, not just a few. Step 11: If you did not get enough right, press Run the sprint again. This is not a punishment! It is practice, like kicking a ball again and again. I expect you to try once more and use what you learned the first time. Step 12: If you want, come and tell me which questions felt hard. We can talk about those together before you run the sprint again. How you will know the page is finished: when one sprint has enough right answers, the page counts it as done. Then you can smile, because your push and pull words are fast now. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me how it goes.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today we are on the Solve Real Problems page. Here you use what you learned about pushes and pulls to answer real questions from home, school and outside. This is why we learn science — so we can explain the world around us. You will need your thinking brain, and maybe a pencil and paper. I expect you to try each one first, before you ask me for help. Let's begin! 1. There are 6 problems on this page. Read the first one slowly, all the way to the end. Then read it again — that is a science habit. Ask yourself: is this asking about a push, a pull, stopping, speed, or which way something goes? I expect you to say the question back in your own words before you answer. If a word is tricky, ask me. 2. Now work out your answer. Type it in the box, then press Check answer. A good answer has two parts: what happens, and why. For example you might write "a pull, because it comes towards me". If your brain says "I don't know", press Hint first and read it, then try again. Do not leave the box empty — a try is always better than nothing. 3. When the page tells you your answer is right, that problem is finished. Then move to the next problem and do the same thing again: read, think, type, press Check answer. Keep going until all 6 are green and done. Take your time — there's no rush. 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. It has the same problems, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Then answer just like before, using the same buttons, Check answer and Hint. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems are marked right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is your work saved — I cannot press it for you, so it must be you! Ready? Tell me what problem 1 says, in your own words, and we will start together.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. On this page you do not just say the answer. You say WHY. You use our science words: push, pull, force, move, stop. Doing this helps the idea stick in your head, and it makes you sound like a real scientist. You need your eyes, your thinking, and a grown-up nearby if typing is tricky. There are 4 things to do. Here they all are. 1. Read the prompt. At the top of the box there is a question, like "A ball is rolling across the floor. What could you do to make it stop?" Under it you will see the key ideas — small words like Push, Pull, Force. Read the question twice. Then read the key words. I expect you to say the question out loud in your own words before you write anything. 2. Write your answer in the box, then press Check scientific ideas. A good answer has three little parts: what you know, the rule you used, and why it makes sense. Like this: "I can put my hand in front of the ball. A push can stop a moving thing. So my hand stops the ball." Try to use at least two key words. If the page says you need more, do not worry — just add one more sentence and press Check scientific ideas again. 3. Press Show model explanation to see a good answer. Read it next to yours. Ask yourself: did I use the key words? Did I say why? I do not want you to copy it. I want you to notice one thing you could add next time. Then do this for all four prompts on the page. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one per slide. Press Start on the first slide. Do the same thing on each slide: write your explanation, press Check scientific ideas, then peek at Show model explanation. When a slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when every prompt has your own explanation with the key ideas in it, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Ready? Let's start with prompt one. Read it to me, and tell me what you think you could do to stop a rolling ball.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today we are learning about Sounds. This page has five short ideas to read, and a few small things to try with your own hands and ears. We do this so you can say how sounds are made, name the part of your body that hears, and tell loud sounds from quiet ones. You will need your ears, your hands, and a quiet place to sit. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: read slowly, try every little test with your own body, and say your answers out loud. There are four things to do on this page. Let's go, one at a time. 1. Read the five concepts, one by one. Start at the top with "Sounds All Around Us". Read it slowly. Then press Listen to hear it read to you. Listening while you read helps the words stick. I expect you to read all five, not just the first one. 2. Try each example out loud with your own things.
