Each concept has a little example at the end. Pluck a rubber band. Hum with your fingers on your throat. Clap once softly, then once firmly. Say what you feel, out loud: "I can feel it shaking!" That fast shaking has a science name — vibration. I expect you to try it, not just read it. 3. When you have read all five concepts, press the button at the bottom that says I studied the concepts. Only press it after you really read them all. That button tells your page that this part is done. I expect you to be honest with yourself here — you are learning for you. 4. Now go to the slides under the page. They show the same five ideas, one idea on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Read that slide, then press the arrow on the right to go to the next one. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. Use the same buttons on every slide, all the way to the end. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I studied the concepts, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. When you are done, come back and tell me one thing: what does something have to do to make a sound? Take your time — there's no rush.

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Science Words page. These are the eight special words for our Sounds unit: Sound, Vibration, Ear, Loud, Quiet, Volume, Listen and Echo. We learn them so you can talk about sounds like a real scientist. Here is what I expect from you: try every word, say each one out loud, and write your own sentence. You will need your voice, your ears, and a grown-up nearby if you want help. There are four steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Look at the first word on the page. Read the word, then read what it means. Now press Listen and hear the word. Listen carefully, then say it with me, slowly. Do this for one word at a time, not all at once. Step 2. Now say that word out loud in a big clear voice. Then say the meaning in your own words, not the page's words. For example, for Ear you might say "it is the part I hear with." Then type a sentence using the word and press Check sentence. Read what the checker tells you. A good sentence shows you know the word, like "My ear helps me hear the birds." Then go back and do Step 1 and Step 2 again for the next word, until all eight words are done. Step 3. When you have done every word, scroll to the bottom. Press the button that says I explored the science words. Only press it when you really did try all eight. That button tells your teacher you finished this part. Step 4. Under the page there is a set of slides. Each slide has one of the same words. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: Listen, say the word, then your sentence and Check sentence. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is done when you have pressed I explored the science words, and the last slide is finished. Then every word has been read, said, and used in your own sentence. Ready? Start with word one, and tell me when you have pressed Listen. Take your time — there's no rush.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 6: Sounds. This page is our very first look at it. It tells you what the unit is about and what you will be able to do by the end. It is short and easy, so let's start with something small. You just need your ears, your eyes, and your voice. There are 3 steps on this page. Here they are. Step 1: Read the Unit Overview. Look at the words on the screen and read them slowly. If you see a little speaker picture, press Listen and let it read to you. Listen right to the end, then read it once more with your eyes. I expect you to find out one thing this unit is about, like sounds around us, or how we hear. Step 2: Say in your own words what you think you will learn. Do not copy the words on the screen. Say it out loud to your grown-up, or type it to me. A good answer sounds like this: "I will learn how sounds are made and how my ears hear them." I expect one or two sentences from you, in your own words. Even a short try is great. Step 3: Press Continue to go to The Lesson. Only press it after you have read the overview and said your sentence. Continue takes you to the next part, where we learn together. I expect you to press it yourself when you feel ready. You will know the page is finished when you have read the overview, said what you think you will learn, and pressed Continue and the next page opens. Here is a little secret about this unit: every single sound in the world comes from something shaking! We will feel that with our own hands soon. Ready? Start with Step 1, then tell me your sentence for Step 2. Take your time — there's no rush.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explore the Concept. Here is what we are doing. You will open four little discoveries about sound. Each one asks you to guess what will happen, then type your idea. Scientists do this all the time — they guess first, then find out. By the end you will know that sounds are made when things shake, and that we hear with our ears. What I expect from you: try your own idea first, in your own words. Do not worry about spelling. A guess is never wrong when you are thinking hard. Have a pencil near you, and your ears ready! There are four steps. Here they all are. Step 1. At the top you will see numbered tabs: 1, 2, 3 and 4. Press tab 1. Read the little story there and look closely at the picture or model. Take your time. I expect you to look for one whole minute and notice what is shaking or making a noise. Step 2. Under the picture there is the discovery question. Read it, then stop and think: what do I already know about shaking and sound? Type your idea in the box, then press Check my idea. A good answer uses our science words: sound, vibration, ear. If it says Look again, do not feel sad — press Hint, read it, and try once more. When it says Exactly!, that tab gets a tick. Well done! Step 3. Now do the same for tabs 2, 3 and 4, one at a time. Press the tab, read, think, type, press Check my idea. I expect a tick on every tab. The page is done when all four questions have been answered right. Step 4. Under the page there is a deck of slides. They have the same discoveries, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons as before: type your idea and press Check my idea, and press Hint if you need help. Then press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. How will you know you are finished? Every tab has a tick, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. That is your work saved — I cannot press it for you, so it must come from you. Ready? Press tab 1 and tell me what you see. Take your time — there's no rush.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. Visual models are pictures and 3D shapes that show our sound ideas. We use them because sound is invisible — we cannot see it, so a picture helps us understand it. By the end, you will be able to name what makes a sound and what we hear with. You need your eyes, your ears, and your finger to press and drag. I expect you to look slowly at each one and say what you notice out loud. There are three parts, and five models to look at. Here we go. 1. Look at model one, Sounds All Around Us. Look at everything in the picture. If it moves, put your finger on it and drag it slowly to turn it around. If it has buttons, press them and watch what changes. Do it well by going slowly, not fast. I expect you to name one sound you can see in the picture, like a bird or a car. 2. Now model two, How We Make Sounds. This one shows shaking. Drag it to turn it, and press its buttons. Look hard at the part that is shaking. That fast shaking has a name — vibration. I expect you to point at the shaking part and say the word vibration. 3. Next, model three, Loud Sounds and Quiet Sounds. Press its buttons to change it from loud to quiet. Watch what looks different each time. I expect you to say which one is loud and which one is quiet, and why you think so. 4. Now model four, How We Hear With Our Ears. Turn it around by dragging, so you see the ear from different sides. While you look, touch your own two ears. I expect you to say this out loud: we hear with our ears. 5. Last one, model five, Sounds Travel, and We Keep Ears Safe. Press its buttons and watch the sound move through the air to the ear. Look at what happens when the sound goes far away. I expect you to tell me if a far sound is loud or quiet. 6. Now read the caption under each model. The caption is the little sentence below the picture. Press Listen and hear it read to you. Do it well by listening all the way to the end, then saying the caption in your own words. 7. When you have looked at all five models and heard all five captions, press the button at the bottom that says I explored the models. Only press it when you really have seen them all — that is you being honest, like a good scientist. You will know the page is finished when you have pressed I explored the models at the bottom. I cannot press it for you, so that part is your job! Ready? Start with model one, and tell me what you notice. 🙂

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is a way to do something step by step, like a recipe. This page has 4 methods about sound. They are The Shaky Rubber Band, The Shaker Tin, The Pillow That Hides Sound, and How We Hear With Our Ears. We do this so you learn how a scientist works: guess first, look carefully, then check your guess. By the end you will be able to say the steps of each method out loud, all by yourself. You need your reading eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want to try the sounds too. Here is what I expect from you: say every step out loud, not just in your head. Go slowly. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the first method on the page. Read its first step. Then say that step out loud in your own words. When you have said it, press Show me the next step. A good job here is reading slowly and saying the words clearly. Step 2. Keep pressing Show me the next step. Say each new step out loud before you press again. Keep going until the page says Method complete. That tells you this method is finished. Step 3. Now do the very same thing for every method on the page. Read a step, say it out loud, press Show me the next step, and keep going until you see Method complete. Do this for all 4 methods. I expect you to finish every one, not just the first. Step 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same methods, one method on each slide. On the first slide, press Start. Then use the same buttons on that slide, just like before, and say each step out loud. Step 5. When one slide is done, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide. The dots show you where you are and how many slides are left. Step 6. Keep going slide by slide, saying the steps out loud each time. On the last slide, press the finish button. That is you telling the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when all 4 methods say Method complete, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. When you are ready, start with the first method and tell me when you see Method complete. I will be right here! 🌟

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Worked Examples page. Worked examples are questions about sounds, with the answer shown too. We do them so you can see how a good answer is built, step by step. What I expect from you is simple: try each question yourself FIRST, then look. You need your ears, your voice, and maybe a pencil. Here are your steps. Step 1. Look at the first worked example. Read the question slowly, out loud if you like. Do not press anything yet. Say your own answer first, even a short one. A good try uses our science words, like sound, vibration, ear, loud and quiet. Step 2. Now press Show worked solution. Read the answer and compare it with what you said. Ask yourself: did I say the same idea? Did I use the same science word? It is fine if you were different — that is how we learn. Step 3. Do the same for every worked example. There are 8 of them. Read, think, then press Show worked solution. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 4. Look at the counter at the top of the page. It shows how many examples you have opened. Keep going until every single one is open, so none are left closed. Step 5. Now scroll down to the slides at the bottom. There is a deck of slides with the same examples, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Step 6. On each slide, do the same good work: read the question, say your answer out loud, then press the button to see the worked solution. The little dots under the slide show you where you are in the deck. Step 7. Press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Do every slide the same way, one at a time. When you reach the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when the counter at the top shows all 8 examples opened, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. I only guide you — you press the buttons, because that is how the page saves your work. Now start with Step 1. Read the first question, and tell me your own answer before you open it. I'm listening!

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice in our Sounds unit. This page gives you 12 short questions about sound. We do it so the big ideas stick: sounds are made when things shake, we hear with our ears, and sounds can be loud or quiet. By the end, you will be able to answer sound questions all by yourself. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your listening ears. A grown-up can sit with you to help you read. Here are the steps. 1. Read the first question slowly. Read it twice. Think about the answer in your head, or say it out loud, or write it on your paper first. I expect you to try before you press anything, even if you are not sure. Take your time — there's no rush. 2. Type your answer in the box, then press Check my answer. Write in a few words, like "the ear" or "loud". If you feel stuck, press Give me a hint. You can get up to three hints. If you are still stuck, press Show next step and it shows you one line of the working to help you along. I expect you to try a hint before you ask for the next step. 3. Do this for every question, one at a time, until each one is right. If an answer is not right, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Read the hint, think again, and try once more. The page is done when all 12 questions are right. I expect you to finish every one, not just the easy ones. 4. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides with the same questions, one question on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Answer it and use the same buttons: Check my answer, Give me a hint, and Show next step. I expect the same careful thinking here as before. 5. When a slide is right, press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you where you are and how many are left. Keep going, one slide at a time. 6. On the last slide, answer it, then press the finish button. Only you can press it, because it saves the work you did. You will know the page is finished when all 12 questions show as right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then come back and tell me one thing you learned about sound. Ready? Start with question one, and tell me your answer when you have it.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today we are on the Quick Reference page for Unit 6: Sounds. This page is like a little card that holds all our big sound ideas in one place. We do it so the words stay in your head: sound, vibration, ear, loud, quiet. By the end, you will be able to say our sound facts in your own words. You need your eyes, your ears, and your voice. Ready? Here are your three steps. Step 1. Read the Quick Reference slowly. Look at the page and read each word part one at a time. Where you see a speaker, press Listen and hear the words said out loud. Read it twice if you like. I expect you to go slowly and not rush. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 2. Say the key facts in your own words. Do not just copy the page. Say things like: sounds are made when things shake, we hear with our ears, a drum is loud, a whisper is quiet. Say each one out loud, in a full sentence. I expect three or four sentences, said in YOUR words. You can say them to your grown-up, or to me right here in the chat. Step 3. Press Reference reviewed at the bottom. Do this only after you have read the page and said your facts out loud. That button tells the page you are finished. I expect you to press it yourself, so your good work is saved. You will know the page is finished when you have read it, said the facts in your own words, and pressed Reference reviewed. Now go and do Step 1, then tell me when you are done. 😊

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Experiments page in Unit 6, Sounds. This page has six hands-on experiments. You will listen, shake, tap and hum, and find out how sounds are made. Sounds happen when things shake very fast. That fast shaking has a science name — vibration. By the end you will be able to say how a sound is made, and tell a loud sound from a quiet one. You will need a pencil, your two ears, and a few safe things from home like a rubber band, a tin, a spoon and a pot. It is a good idea to have a grown-up nearby to help you find them. Here is what I expect from you: try each experiment for real, look and listen carefully, and write what you noticed in your own words. Nothing needs to be perfect. Honest noticing is the best science. There are 4 things to do on this page. Here they all are. 1. Read each experiment, then get your things. Each experiment tells you what to use and what to do. Read it slowly, and press Listen to hear it read to you. Listening helps you catch any word you missed. Then go and get the things it names, and put them on the table in front of you. I expect you to have everything ready before you start, so you do not have to stop in the middle. 2. Do the activity, then write in the box. Really do it — pluck the rubber band, tap the tin, hum with your fingers on your throat. Watch and listen carefully while it happens. Then write your answer, or what you noticed, in the box. A good answer says what you did and what happened, like "I plucked the band and it shook, and I heard a sound." Try to use our science words: sound, vibration, loud, quiet, ear. 3. Press Mark complete under each activity. When you have done one experiment and written in its box, press Mark complete under that activity. Do this for every one of the six. When all six are marked, press Finish activities at the bottom of the page. I expect you to press Mark complete only after you have really done the experiment, not before. 4. Do the slides at the bottom of the page. Under the page there is a deck of slides. Each slide has one of the same experiments on it. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide as you did above, so read, listen, do, and write. Then press the arrow on the right to go to the next slide. The little dots under the slide show you where you are, so you can see how many are left. On the last slide, press Finish activities. You will know the page is finished when every activity has Mark complete pressed, you have pressed Finish activities at the bottom, and you have reached the last slide and pressed Finish activities there too. Let's start with something small. Go and find your rubber band and your tin, then tell me when you have them, and we will begin experiment one together.

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Sound Games. These games ask you quick questions about Unit 6, all about sounds, ears and vibrations. We play them so the words stick in your head, like a song you remember. You do not need a pencil. You just need your eyes, your fingers, and your best thinking. Here is what to do. 1. Look at the games on your screen and pick one. Press Start game. A question will pop up with some answers to choose from. Read the question slowly, then tap the answer you think is right. Every time you get a round right, you win a star! I expect you to think for a moment before you tap — no fast guessing. If you are not sure, press the clue and it will help you. 2. When the game ends, press Play again. This lets you win more stars. A game is mastered when it has all of its stars. That means you got every round right. I expect you to keep trying that same game until all its stars are shining. If you get one wrong, that is fine — read the little explanation, then play again and use what you learned. 3. Now do the same for every game on the page. Press Start game on the next one, answer the rounds, and press Play again until it is mastered too. Keep going, game by game, until every game has all its stars. I expect you to take your time and be kind to yourself. Take a breath if a question feels tricky. You will know the page is finished when every game is mastered — the page finishes by itself when all the stars are won. You do not need to press anything extra at the end. Off you go and press Start game on your first game. Tell me when you have played your first round, and tell me one question you got right!

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Solve Real Problems" page. This page gives you real-life sound puzzles, like a drum being hit or a very loud noise near your ears. We do it so you can use what you know about sound, vibration and ears in real life, not just in words. By the end you will be able to explain why sounds happen and how to keep your ears safe. You need your eyes, your ears, and your thinking brain. Here are all the steps. 1. Look at the page. There are 6 problems, one at a time. Read the problem slowly. Then read it again. Ask yourself: what is this question really asking me? I expect you to know what the question wants before you start typing. 2. Now think of your answer in your head. Say it quietly to yourself first. Then type it in the box. A good answer tells the thing AND the why, like "it makes a sound because something is shaking." Then press Check answer. 3. If your brain feels stuck, that is okay. Press Hint. The hint gives you a little clue, not the answer. Read the clue, then try typing again. I expect you to try your own answer first, before the hint. 4. When the page says your answer is right, that problem is done. Well done! Move on to the next problem and do the same three things: read, think, type, press Check answer. 5. Keep going until all 6 problems say right. Take your time — there's no rush. If one is tricky, press Hint and try again. Mistakes are how we learn. 6. Now look under the page. There is a deck of slides. It has the same problems, one problem on each slide. This is your practice round. 7. On the first slide, press Start. Then answer just like before: think, type your answer, press Check answer. Press Hint if you need a clue. 8. When that slide is right, press the arrow on the right. That takes you to the next slide. Look at the little dots under the slide — they show you which slide you are on. 9. Keep going slide by slide. Same buttons every time: type, Check answer, Hint if stuck, then the arrow on the right. 10. On the last slide, press the finish button. That tells the page you are done. You will know the page is finished when all 6 problems say your answer is right, and you have pressed the finish button on the last slide. Then come back and tell me one thing you learned about sound. I will be right here. 🙂

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Science Fluency. Let's look at that together. Science Fluency is a quick sound sprint. You get 12 short questions about Unit 6, all about sounds. You answer them fast, one after the other. A timer at the top counts your time. Why do we do this? Because when you know something really well, the answer comes out fast. This helps your sound words stick in your head, like your name does. What you need: your eyes on the screen, your hands ready to type, and a calm quiet spot. A grown-up can sit near you to help you type. What I expect from you: try every question, even the tricky ones. Use short answers, like "ears" or "loud" or "vibrating". Guess your best guess if you are not sure. Speed is nice, but being right matters more. Here are your steps. Step 1. Press the button to start the sprint. The first question will pop up. Read it slowly, even though it is a sprint. Reading it right helps you answer it right. Step 2. Type your answer in the box. Keep it short. One or two words is plenty for most of these. Step 3. Press Check & continue. This checks your answer and brings the next question. Do this for every question, all the way to question 12. Step 4. Keep going without stopping. If one question feels hard, put your best answer and press Check & continue anyway. Do not sit and worry — you can meet that question again next time. Step 5. When the 12 questions are done, look at your score. You need most of them right to finish the page. Take a happy breath — you just did 12 questions! Step 6. If you did not get enough right, that is okay. Mistakes are how we learn. Press Run the sprint again and do the 12 questions one more time. You will be faster and surer this time. Step 7. The page is finished when one sprint has enough right answers. The page will show you that you are done. That is how you know you can stop. One little tip from me: remember the big idea. Sounds happen when something shakes, and we hear with our ears. Lots of the questions come from that. Ready? Press start and begin question one. Come back and tell me how it went!

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the "Explain Your Thinking" page. On this page you say WHY, not just what. You will talk about sounds and use our science words: sound, vibration, ear, loud, quiet. Doing this helps the ideas stick in your head for a long time. You need your eyes to read, your hands to type, and maybe a grown-up nearby to help with spelling. Here is what I expect from you. Try your own words first. Do not worry about perfect writing. Just tell me what you know and why. There are 4 steps. Here they all are. Step 1: Read the first prompt. There are 4 prompts on this page. Under each one there are key ideas — those are the science words you should use. Read the prompt slowly. Then say the answer out loud to yourself before you write. Good thinking sounds like this: "A whisper is quiet, because the shaking is very small."

Step 2: Write in the box, then press Check scientific ideas. Write what you know, then write why. Try to use the key words. For example: "I hear with my ear. The drum shakes, and the shaking is a vibration." If the page asks for more, add one more sentence and press Check scientific ideas again. I expect at least two sentences from you: what happens, and why. Step 3: Press Show model explanation. This opens a good answer so you can compare it with yours. Look for words you used the same. Look for one word you forgot. You do not copy it — you just check. Then do steps 1, 2 and 3 again for the other prompts, until all 4 use the key ideas. Step 4: Do the slides at the bottom. Under the page is a deck of slides with the same prompts, one on each slide. Press Start on the first slide. Use the same buttons on each slide: write, then Check scientific ideas, then Show model explanation. Press the arrow on the right to move to the next slide. The little dots under the slide tell you where you are. On the last slide, press the finish button. You will know the page is finished when all 4 explanations use the key ideas, and the dots show you reached the last slide and pressed finish. Now let's start with step 1. Read the first prompt and tell me what you think. Take your time — there's no rush.
